split turns a string into a list; join (called on the separator) turns a list back into a string. Together they solve many text tasks.

Checking content

print("12345".isdigit())     # True
print("hello".isalpha())     # True
print("abc123".isalnum())    # True
print("   ".isspace())       # True
print("Hello".istitle())     # True

Useful for simple validation, e.g. checking a PIN code is all digits.

f-strings in depth

name = "Meera"
price = 1499.5
qty = 3
ratio = 0.4567

print(f"{name} bought {qty} items")
print(f"Total: ₹{price * qty:,.2f}")   # ₹4,498.50
print(f"Ratio: {ratio:.1%}")           # 45.7%
print(f"|{name:<10}|")                 # left-align in 10 characters
print(f"|{name:>10}|")                 # right-align
print(f"|{name:^10}|")                 # centre
print(f"{7:03d}")                      # 007: zero-padded
print(f"{name.upper()} has {len(name)} letters")

Format specs after the colon: , (thousands separator), .2f (2 decimals), % (percentage), < > ^ (alignment and width), 03d (zero-padding). Alignment is perfect for printing simple tables.

Looping over a string

word = "banana"
vowels = 0
for letter in word:
    if letter in "aeiou":
        vowels += 1
print(f"{word} has {vowels} vowels")

Comparing strings

print("apple" == "apple")        # True
print("Apple" == "apple")        # False: case matters
print("Apple".lower() == "apple".lower())  # True
print("apple" < "banana")        # True: alphabetical

For case-insensitive comparisons of international text, .casefold() is more thorough than .lower().

A practical example: make a URL slug

def slugify(title):
    cleaned = "".join(ch if ch.isalnum() or ch == " " else "" for ch in title)
    return "-".join(cleaned.lower().split())

print(slugify("  Python Strings: The Complete Basics! "))
# python-strings-the-complete-basics

The ch for ch in title part is a generator expression, a compact loop you'll understand better after the Lists and Loops lessons.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting strings are immutable: name.upper() alone does nothing visible; assign the result.
  • Off-by-one slices: s[0:3] gives 3 characters, indexes 0, 1, 2.
  • Case-sensitive comparisons and replacements.
  • Joining non-strings: ", ".join([1, 2]) fails; convert first: ", ".join(map(str, [1, 2])).

Exercise

  1. Take " hello WORLD " and turn it into "Hello world".
  2. Print the first 3 and last 3 characters of your full name.
  3. Check if a word is a palindrome using slicing (word == word[::-1]).
  4. Count how many times "the" appears in a sentence, ignoring case.
  5. Turn "red,green,blue" into "RED / GREEN / BLUE".
  6. Print a 3-row table of names and scores, aligned with f-string widths.

Summary

  • Index with s[i], slice with s[start:stop:step]; indexes start at 0, negatives count from the end.
  • Strings are immutable; methods return new strings.
  • Key methods: strip, lower/upper, replace, split, join, find, count, startswith.
  • f-strings with format specs handle numbers, percentages and alignment.

Next, you'll work with numbers and maths in Python.
item.excerpt:encoded: Create strings, index and slice them, use the essential string methods, format text with f-strings, and loop over characters.

item.title: Python Numbers
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Python is a favourite language for anything involving numbers, from shopping carts to scientific research. This lesson covers Python's number types, arithmetic, rounding, and the modules that handle maths, randomness and money.

int and float

students = 32          # int
average = 78.5         # float
big = 1_000_000        # underscores make big numbers readable
print(students, average, big)
print(type(students), type(average))
  • int: whole numbers of any size. 2 ** 200 works fine.
  • float: decimal numbers with about 15–17 digits of precision.
  • An operation with a float gives a float: 3 + 2.0 is 5.0.

Arithmetic operators

a, b = 17, 5
print(a + b)    # 22
print(a - b)    # 12
print(a * b)    # 85
print(a / b)    # 3.4: true division, always a float
print(a // b)   # 3: floor division
print(a % b)    # 2: remainder
print(a ** b)   # 1419857: power
print(-a // b)  # -4: floor division rounds DOWN, towards minus infinity

// and % are very useful together:

total_seconds = 3725
hours = total_seconds // 3600
minutes = (total_seconds % 3600) // 60
seconds = total_seconds % 60
print(f"{hours}h {minutes}m {seconds}s")   # 1h 2m 5s

print(divmod(17, 5))   # (3, 2): quotient and remainder in one step

Operator precedence follows maths rules: ** first, then * / // %, then + -. Use brackets when in doubt.

Float precision

print(0.1 + 0.2)              # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)       # False

import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))  # True

Like in every language, binary floats can't store some decimals exactly. Compare floats with math.isclose(), round when displaying, and use Decimal for money (below).

Rounding

print(round(3.14159, 2))   # 3.14
print(round(7.5))          # 8
print(round(2.5))          # 2 (!)
print(round(3.5))          # 4

import math
print(math.floor(4.7))     # 4: always down
print(math.ceil(4.2))      # 5: always up
print(math.trunc(-4.7))    # -4: drop the decimals

round() uses banker's rounding: exact halves round to the nearest even number, so round(2.5) is 2. This avoids bias in large statistics, but surprises people. For "school" rounding of money, use Decimal.

math.ceil is ideal for counting pages or boxes: 47 items at 10 per page need math.ceil(47 / 10) = 5 pages.

Useful built-in functions

numbers = [12, 7, 25, 3]
print(abs(-9))          # 9
print(min(numbers))     # 3
print(max(numbers))     # 25
print(sum(numbers))     # 47
print(sum(numbers) / len(numbers))  # 11.75: average
print(pow(2, 8))        # 256

The math module

import math

print(math.sqrt(144))         # 12.0
print(math.pi)                # 3.141592653589793
print(math.factorial(5))      # 120
print(math.gcd(24, 36))       # 12
print(math.log10(1000))       # 3.0
print(round(math.sin(math.pi / 2), 2))  # 1.0

radius = 7
area = math.pi * radius ** 2
print(f"Circle area: {area:.2f}")       # 153.94

import math loads the module; you'll learn more about modules in lesson 14.

Random numbers

import random

print(random.randint(1, 6))          # a dice roll: 1 to 6 inclusive
print(random.random())               # float from 0.0 up to 1.0
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))

cards = ["A", "K", "Q", "J"]
random.shuffle(cards)
print(cards)
print(random.sample(range(1, 50), 6))  # 6 unique lottery numbers

For passwords, tokens or anything security-related, use the secrets module instead: secrets.token_hex(16).

Exact decimals for money: Decimal

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

price = Decimal("19.99")
qty = 3
total = price * qty
print(total)                         # 59.97 exactly

print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2"))   # 0.3 exactly

tax = (total * Decimal("0.18")).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
print(tax)                           # 10.79
print(Decimal("2.5").quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))  # 3
  • Create Decimals from strings (Decimal("19.99")), not floats, or the float's imprecision comes along.
  • quantize rounds to a fixed number of places with the rounding rule you choose.

Banks, shops and accounting software use Decimal (or store amounts as whole paise/cents in ints).

Converting and validating numbers

print(int("42"), float("3.5"), int(3.99))   # 42 3.5 3
print(int("ff", 16))                        # 255: from hexadecimal
print(bin(10), hex(255))                    # 0b1010 0xff

text = "12a"
if text.isdigit():
    print(int(text))
else:
    print(f"'{text}' is not a whole number")

Formatting numbers

amount = 1234567.891
print(f"{amount:,.2f}")     # 1,234,567.89
print(f"{0.256:.1%}")       # 25.6%
print(f"{42:05d}")          # 00042
print(f"{1500000:.2e}")     # 1.50e+06

For Indian-style grouping (12,34,567) or currency symbols for any country, the third-party babel package handles locale-aware formatting.

Common mistakes

  • **Comparing floats with ==.** Use math.isclose.
  • **Expecting round(2.5) to be 3.**
  • Floats for money in serious applications. Use Decimal or integer paise.
  • **Decimal(0.1)** instead of Decimal("0.1").
  • Integer vs true division confusion: / always returns a float in Python 3.

Exercise

  1. Convert 500 minutes into hours and minutes using // and %.
  2. Calculate the area and circumference of a circle with radius 10, rounded to 2 decimals.
  3. Simulate rolling two dice 5 times and print each total.
  4. Calculate 3 items at ₹19.99 plus 18% tax using Decimal, rounded to 2 places.
  5. Find how many pages you need for 123 search results at 20 per page.

Summary

  • int for whole numbers, float for decimals; / gives floats, // floors, % gives remainders.
  • Floats can be imprecise: compare with math.isclose, use Decimal for money.
  • round() uses banker's rounding; math.floor/ceil always go down/up.
  • The math, random, decimal and secrets modules extend Python's number skills.

Next, you'll store collections of values in lists.
item.excerpt:encoded: Integers and floats, all arithmetic operators, rounding, the math and random modules, exact money calculations with Decimal, and formatting numbers.

item.title: Python Lists
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A list is an ordered collection of items: a to-do list, a playlist, a set of exam scores. Lists are the most used data structure in Python, and they're very flexible: they can grow, shrink, be sorted and hold any kind of value.

Creating lists

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
scores = [92, 87, 95, 78]
mixed = ["Asha", 21, True, None]
empty = []
letters = list("abc")       # ['a', 'b', 'c']
numbers = list(range(1, 6)) # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

print(fruits, len(fruits))
print(numbers)

Indexing and slicing

Lists use the same indexing and slicing as strings:

colours = ["red", "green", "blue", "yellow", "purple"]
print(colours[0])     # red
print(colours[-1])    # purple
print(colours[1:3])   # ['green', 'blue']
print(colours[:2])    # ['red', 'green']
print(colours[::-1])  # reversed copy

Lists are mutable

Unlike strings, you can change a list in place:

tasks = ["wake up", "code", "sleep"]
tasks[1] = "code in Python"
print(tasks)

Adding items

cart = ["pen"]
cart.append("notebook")            # add one item to the end
cart.insert(0, "bag")              # insert at a position
cart.extend(["eraser", "ruler"])   # add several items
print(cart)   # ['bag', 'pen', 'notebook', 'eraser', 'ruler']

combined = [1, 2] + [3, 4]         # + makes a new list
print(combined)

append([1, 2]) would add the list as one item; extend adds each item separately.

Removing items

items = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "b"]

items.remove("b")      # removes the FIRST "b"
print(items)           # ['a', 'c', 'd', 'b']

last = items.pop()     # removes and returns the last item
print(last, items)     # b ['a', 'c', 'd']

first = items.pop(0)   # removes and returns item at index 0
print(first, items)    # a ['c', 'd']

del items[0]           # delete by index
print(items)           # ['d']

items.clear()          # remove everything
print(items)           # []

remove raises a ValueError if the item isn't there, so check with in first when unsure.

Searching

langs = ["python", "sql", "javascript", "sql"]
print("sql" in langs)        # True
print(langs.index("sql"))    # 1: first position
print(langs.count("sql"))    # 2

Sorting

nums = [42, 7, 19, 3]
nums.sort()                  # sorts the list in place
print(nums)                  # [3, 7, 19, 42]
nums.sort(reverse=True)
print(nums)                  # [42, 19, 7, 3]

names = ["rohan", "Asha", "meera"]
print(sorted(names))                  # ['Asha', 'meera', 'rohan']: capitals first
print(sorted(names, key=str.lower))   # ['Asha', 'meera', 'rohan']: case-insensitive
print(sorted(names, key=len))         # ['Asha', 'rohan', 'meera']: by length
print(names)                          # unchanged: sorted() returns a new list
  • list.sort() changes the list and returns None.
  • sorted(list) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone.
  • key= sorts by a calculated value; very powerful with lists of dictionaries (lesson 10).

A common bug: nums = nums.sort() sets nums to None.

Looping over lists

scores = [72, 95, 88]

for score in scores:
    print(score)

for position, score in enumerate(scores, start=1):
    print(f"{position}. {score}")

names = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name}: {score}")
  • enumerate gives you the position along with each item.
  • zip walks through several lists side by side.

Built-in functions with lists

scores = [72, 95, 88, 64]
print(len(scores), sum(scores), min(scores), max(scores))
print(f"Average: {sum(scores) / len(scores):.1f}")
print(any(s < 65 for s in scores))   # True: is any score below 65?
print(all(s >= 60 for s in scores))  # True: are all scores at least 60?

Copying lists

original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original           # NOT a copy: same list, two names
copy1 = original.copy()    # a real copy
copy2 = original[:]        # also a copy
copy3 = list(original)     # also a copy

original.append(4)
print(alias)   # [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(copy1)   # [1, 2, 3]

These are shallow copies: if the list contains other lists, those inner lists are still shared. Use copy.deepcopy() for a full copy of nested data.

List comprehensions

A compact way to build a new list from another:

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

squares = [n * n for n in numbers]
evens = [n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
labels = [f"Item {n}" for n in numbers[:3]]

print(squares)   # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36]
print(evens)     # [2, 4, 6]
print(labels)    # ['Item 1', 'Item 2', 'Item 3']

Read [n * n for n in numbers if n > 2] as "n squared, for each n in numbers, if n is greater than 2". The same with a loop:

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
result = []
for n in numbers:
    if n > 2:
        result.append(n * n)
print(result)    # [9, 16, 25, 36]

Comprehensions are idiomatic Python. Keep them short; if one gets complicated, use a normal loop.

Nested lists

grid = [
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
    [7, 8, 9],
]
print(grid[1][2])                     # 6: row 1, column 2
print([row[0] for row in grid])       # [1, 4, 7]: first column

Unpacking

first, second, *rest = ["gold", "silver", "bronze", "4th", "5th"]
print(first, second, rest)   # gold silver ['bronze', '4th', '5th']

Common mistakes

  • **nums = nums.sort()**, which sets nums to None.
  • **b = a thinking it copies.**
  • Changing a list while looping over it (removing items skips elements). Loop over a copy or build a new list with a comprehension.
  • **IndexError** from using an index equal to len(list).

Exercise

  1. Create a list of five cities. Add one, insert one at the start, and remove the third.
  2. Sort a list of numbers in descending order without changing the original.
  3. From [3, 8, 12, 5, 20, 7], make a list of only the numbers over 6, doubled, with a comprehension.
  4. Print a numbered shopping list with enumerate.
  5. Given two lists of names and ages, print "Name is Age" using zip.

Summary

  • Lists are ordered and mutable; index and slice them like strings.
  • append, insert, extend add; remove, pop, del, clear remove.
  • sort() changes the list; sorted() returns a new one; use key= for custom order.
  • Copy with .copy(); build lists concisely with comprehensions.

Next, you'll meet two more collections: tuples and sets.
item.excerpt:encoded: Create, index, slice and change lists; add, remove, sort and search items; copy lists safely; and write list comprehensions.

item.title: Python Tuples and Sets
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Lists are great general-purpose collections, but Python has two more that are better for specific jobs. Tuples hold a fixed group of values that shouldn't change. Sets hold unique items and answer "is this in here?" extremely fast.

Tuples

A tuple is like a list that can't be changed after it's created. It's written with round brackets:

point = (10, 20)
rgb = (37, 99, 235)
person = ("Asha", 21, "Pune")

print(point[0])      # 10
print(person[-1])    # Pune
print(len(rgb))      # 3
print(rgb[0:2])      # (37, 99)

Indexing, slicing, len, in, count and index all work just like with lists. What you can't do is change it:

point = (10, 20)
# point[0] = 15       # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
point = (15, 20)      # you can make a new tuple and reassign the name
print(point)

The comma makes the tuple

a = (5)      # just the number 5 in brackets
b = (5,)     # a tuple with one item
c = 5, 6     # brackets are optional
print(type(a), type(b), type(c))

Tuple unpacking

Tuples shine when you unpack them into variables:

person = ("Meera", 24, "Jaipur")
name, age, city = person
print(f"{name} ({age}) lives in {city}")

# Functions can return several values as a tuple
def min_max(numbers):
    return min(numbers), max(numbers)

low, high = min_max([7, 2, 9, 4])
print(low, high)   # 2 9

# Swapping uses tuple packing and unpacking
x, y = 1, 2
x, y = y, x
print(x, y)

When to use a tuple instead of a list

  • The data is a fixed record whose positions have meaning: coordinates (x, y), an RGB colour, a date (2024, 5, 1), a database row.
  • You want to protect the data from accidental changes.
  • You need it as a dictionary key or set item (lists can't be keys because they're mutable).
distances = {
    ("Pune", "Mumbai"): 150,
    ("Delhi", "Agra"): 233,
}
print(distances[("Pune", "Mumbai")])

A rule of thumb: lists for many items of the same kind; tuples for a few items of different kinds that belong together.

Named tuples

When positions get confusing, give them names:

from collections import namedtuple

Product = namedtuple("Product", ["name", "price", "stock"])
pen = Product("Pen set", 250, 30)
print(pen.name, pen.price)   # readable access by name
print(pen[1])                # still works by index

Sets

A set is an unordered collection of unique items, written with curly braces:

tags = {"python", "sql", "python", "html"}
print(tags)          # {'python', 'sql', 'html'}: duplicate removed, order not guaranteed
print(len(tags))     # 3

Removing duplicates

The most common use of sets:

cities = ["Pune", "Delhi", "Pune", "Jaipur", "Delhi"]
unique = set(cities)
print(unique)              # 3 unique cities
print(sorted(unique))      # ['Delhi', 'Jaipur', 'Pune']: as a sorted list

# Keep the original order while removing duplicates:
print(list(dict.fromkeys(cities)))   # ['Pune', 'Delhi', 'Jaipur']

Fast membership tests

banned_words = {"spam", "scam", "free money"}
message = "this is not spam"

print("spam" in message.split())   # True
print("hello" in banned_words)     # False

Checking in on a list looks at every item one by one. A set uses hashing and finds the answer almost instantly, even with millions of items. If you check membership often, use a set.

Adding and removing

skills = {"html", "css"}
skills.add("javascript")
skills.update(["python", "sql"])
skills.discard("css")      # no error if missing
# skills.remove("java")    # KeyError if missing
print(skills)

Sets have no indexes (skills[0] is an error), because they have no order.

Empty set: {} creates an empty dictionary. Use set() for an empty set.

Set operations

python_devs = {"Asha", "Rohan", "Meera", "Kabir"}
sql_devs = {"Meera", "Kabir", "Sara"}

print(python_devs | sql_devs)   # union: knows either
print(python_devs & sql_devs)   # intersection: knows both → {'Meera', 'Kabir'}
print(python_devs - sql_devs)   # difference: Python but not SQL → {'Asha', 'Rohan'}
print(python_devs ^ sql_devs)   # symmetric difference: exactly one of them

print({"Meera"} <= sql_devs)    # subset check: True

The same operations exist as methods: union, intersection, difference, issubset.

A practical example

yesterday = {"asha@x.com", "rohan@x.com", "meera@x.com"}
today = {"rohan@x.com", "meera@x.com", "kabir@x.com"}

print("New subscribers:", today - yesterday)
print("Unsubscribed:", yesterday - today)
print("Stayed:", len(today & yesterday))

Comparing two lists of ids or emails is a one-liner with sets.

What can go in a set

Set items (and dictionary keys) must be hashable: immutable types like numbers, strings and tuples. Lists and dictionaries can't go in a set. frozenset is an immutable set, which can itself go in a set.

Choosing a collection

Common mistakes

  • **(5) instead of (5,)** for a one-item tuple.
  • **{} for an empty set** (it's a dict).
  • Expecting a set to keep order or support indexing.
  • Putting lists into sets → TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.

Exercise

  1. Create a tuple for a book (title, author, year) and unpack it into three variables.
  2. Write a function that returns the average and the highest of a list as a tuple, and unpack the result.
  3. Remove duplicates from [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 5] and print them sorted.
  4. Given two sets of students in two clubs, print who is in both, who is in only the first, and everyone.
  5. Check whether a username is in a set of 5 reserved names.

Summary

  • Tuples are ordered and immutable; great for fixed records, unpacking and dictionary keys.
  • Sets hold unique, unordered items; great for removing duplicates and fast in checks.
  • Set operations |, &, -, ^ compare collections in one line.
  • set() makes an empty set; {} makes an empty dict.

Next, you'll learn dictionaries: Python's key–value collection.
item.excerpt:encoded: Use tuples for fixed groups of values and unpacking, and sets for unique items, fast membership tests and set operations like union and intersection.

item.title: Python Dictionaries
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A dictionary (dict) stores data as key–value pairs: a word and its meaning, a product and its price, a setting and its value. You look values up by key instead of by position. Dictionaries are everywhere in Python, and they map directly to JSON, the data format of the web.

Creating dictionaries

user = {
    "name": "Asha",
    "age": 21,
    "city": "Pune",
    "skills": ["Python", "SQL"],
}

prices = {"pen": 20, "notebook": 60, "bag": 899}
empty = {}
from_pairs = dict(name="Rohan", age=25)

print(user)
print(len(prices))     # 3

Keys are usually strings, but can be any immutable value (numbers, tuples). Values can be anything, including lists and other dictionaries. Since Python 3.7, dictionaries keep the order in which keys were added.

Reading values

user = {"name": "Asha", "age": 21}

print(user["name"])                 # Asha
# print(user["email"])              # KeyError: 'email'

print(user.get("email"))            # None: no error
print(user.get("email", "not set")) # not set: default value
print("age" in user)                # True: checks keys

Use dict[key] when the key must exist (a missing key is a bug), and .get(key, default) when it might be missing.

Adding, changing and deleting

stock = {"pen": 40, "notebook": 12}

stock["eraser"] = 25          # add a new key
stock["pen"] = 35             # change an existing value
stock["notebook"] += 10       # update based on the old value

del stock["eraser"]           # delete a key (KeyError if missing)
removed = stock.pop("pen")    # delete and return the value
print(removed, stock)         # 35 {'notebook': 22}

stock.update({"ruler": 15, "notebook": 30})  # add/overwrite several keys
print(stock)

Looping over dictionaries

scores = {"Asha": 92, "Rohan": 78, "Meera": 85}

for name in scores:                  # loops over keys
    print(name)

for score in scores.values():
    print(score)

for name, score in scores.items():   # keys and values together
    print(f"{name}: {score}")

print(list(scores.keys()))

.items() is the most common way to loop over a dictionary.

Sorting by value

scores = {"Asha": 92, "Rohan": 78, "Meera": 85}

ranking = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
for position, (name, score) in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
    print(f"{position}. {name} – {score}")

print(max(scores, key=scores.get))   # Asha: key with the highest value

lambda item: item[1] is a tiny inline function that returns the value of each (key, value) pair; you'll learn lambdas in the Functions lesson.

Nested data

Real data is often dictionaries inside lists inside dictionaries, exactly like JSON from an API:

order = {
    "id": 1042,
    "customer": {"name": "Rohan", "city": "Delhi"},
    "items": [
        {"product": "Notebook", "price": 120, "qty": 3},
        {"product": "Pen set", "price": 250, "qty": 1},
    ],
    "paid": True,
}

print(order["customer"]["city"])          # Delhi
print(order["items"][0]["product"])       # Notebook

total = sum(item["price"] * item["qty"] for item in order["items"])
print(f"Order {order['id']} total: ₹{total}")   # ₹610

Notice order['id'] with single quotes inside the double-quoted f-string.

A list of dictionaries

The most common shape for tabular data:

students = [
    {"name": "Asha", "score": 92, "city": "Pune"},
    {"name": "Rohan", "score": 78, "city": "Delhi"},
    {"name": "Meera", "score": 85, "city": "Pune"},
]

top = [s["name"] for s in students if s["score"] >= 80]
print(top)                                         # ['Asha', 'Meera']

by_score = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s["score"], reverse=True)
print([s["name"] for s in by_score])               # ['Asha', 'Meera', 'Rohan']

average = sum(s["score"] for s in students) / len(students)
print(f"Average: {average:.1f}")                   # 85.0

Counting and grouping

Counting how often things appear is a classic dictionary task:

words = "the cat and the dog and the bird".split()

counts = {}
for word in words:
    counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
print(counts)   # {'the': 3, 'cat': 1, 'and': 2, 'dog': 1, 'bird': 1}

from collections import Counter
print(Counter(words).most_common(2))   # [('the', 3), ('and', 2)]

Grouping items by a key:

students = [
    {"name": "Asha", "city": "Pune"},
    {"name": "Rohan", "city": "Delhi"},
    {"name": "Meera", "city": "Pune"},
]

by_city = {}
for s in students:
    by_city.setdefault(s["city"], []).append(s["name"])
print(by_city)   # {'Pune': ['Asha', 'Meera'], 'Delhi': ['Rohan']}

setdefault(key, default) returns the value for the key, first inserting the default if the key is missing. (collections.defaultdict(list) does the same job.)

Dictionary comprehensions

prices = {"pen": 20, "notebook": 60, "bag": 899}

with_tax = {item: round(price * 1.18, 2) for item, price in prices.items()}
cheap = {item: price for item, price in prices.items() if price < 100}
squares = {n: n * n for n in range(1, 6)}

print(with_tax)
print(cheap)     # {'pen': 20, 'notebook': 60}
print(squares)   # {1: 1, 2: 4, 3: 9, 4: 16, 5: 25}

Merging and copying

defaults = {"theme": "light", "font_size": 16}
user_settings = {"theme": "dark"}

settings = defaults | user_settings      # Python 3.9+: later values win
print(settings)                          # {'theme': 'dark', 'font_size': 16}

copy = settings.copy()                   # shallow copy
copy["theme"] = "blue"
print(settings["theme"])                 # still dark

Common mistakes

  • **KeyError** from d[key] on a missing key; use .get() or check with in.
  • Looping and changing size: adding or deleting keys while looping over a dict raises an error. Loop over list(d) instead.
  • Using mutable values as keys (lists) → TypeError.
  • **Expecting in to check values**: "Asha" in scores.values() checks values; plain in checks keys.

Exercise

  1. Create a dictionary of five countries and their capitals. Print each as "Capital of X is Y".
  2. Write a word-frequency counter for a sentence of your choice, ignoring case.
  3. Given a list of product dicts with name, category and price, group the names by category.
  4. Find the most expensive product with max(..., key=...).
  5. Make a dict comprehension that maps each word in a list to its length.

Summary

  • Dictionaries map keys to values; read with d[key] or safely with d.get(key, default).
  • Add or change with d[key] = value; remove with del or pop.
  • Loop with .items(); sort with sorted(d.items(), key=...).
  • Lists of dicts model tables and JSON; Counter, setdefault and comprehensions make counting and grouping easy.

Next, you'll make decisions with if, elif and else.
item.excerpt:encoded: Store key-value data in dictionaries: read safely with get, add, update and delete keys, loop over items, nest data, count things, and use dictionary comprehensions.

item.title: Python If/Else
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Programs become useful when they can decide: approve or reject, show a warning or not, charge shipping or give it free. Python's if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is true.

if

temperature = 34

if temperature > 30:
    print("It's hot today.")
    print("Remember to drink water.")

print("Have a nice day.")

The condition is followed by a colon, and the block is indented. If the condition is false, the indented lines are skipped.

else and elif

age = 16

if age >= 18:
    print("You can vote.")
else:
    print(f"You can vote in {18 - age} years.")

For more than two options, use elif ("else if"):

score = 76

if score >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 75:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 60:
    grade = "C"
elif score >= 40:
    grade = "D"
else:
    grade = "F"

print(f"Score {score}: grade {grade}")   # Score 76: grade B

Python checks each condition from the top and runs only the first block whose condition is true. That's why the order matters: 95 is also >= 75, but it's caught by the first condition.

Comparison operators

Python lets you chain comparisons, just like in maths:

age = 25
if 18 <= age < 60:
    print("Working age")

and, or, not

age = 22
has_ticket = True
is_vip = False

if age >= 18 and has_ticket:
    print("Welcome to the concert.")

if is_vip or age < 12:
    print("Free entry.")
else:
    print("Standard entry.")

if not has_ticket:
    print("Please buy a ticket.")

Python uses the words and, or and not instead of symbols. and is evaluated before or; use brackets to make mixed conditions clear.

Truthy checks

Empty strings, empty collections, 0 and None count as false:

username = "   ".strip()
cart = []

if not username:
    print("Please enter a username.")

if cart:
    print(f"{len(cart)} items in cart")
else:
    print("Your cart is empty.")

This is the Pythonic way: write if cart: rather than if len(cart) > 0:.

Membership: in

day = "sat"
if day in ("sat", "sun"):
    print("Weekend!")

email = "asha@example.com"
if "@" not in email:
    print("Invalid email")
else:
    print("Looks like an email")

in works with strings, lists, tuples, sets and dictionary keys, and replaces long chains of or.

Identity: is

Use is to compare with None (and True/False in rare cases):

result = None
if result is None:
    print("No result yet.")

== asks "are these equal?"; is asks "is this the very same object?". For None, always use is.

Nested conditions and guard clauses

Nested ifs work but get hard to read:

def can_checkout(user, cart):
    if user is not None:
        if cart:
            if user.get("address"):
                return "OK"
            else:
                return "Add an address"
        else:
            return "Cart is empty"
    else:
        return "Please log in"

print(can_checkout({"address": "Pune"}, ["book"]))

The same logic with guard clauses (return early on problems):

def can_checkout(user, cart):
    if user is None:
        return "Please log in"
    if not cart:
        return "Cart is empty"
    if not user.get("address"):
        return "Add an address"
    return "OK"

print(can_checkout({"address": "Pune"}, []))
print(can_checkout(None, ["book"]))

Flat code is easier to read and extend. (You'll learn def and return in the Functions lesson.)

Conditional expressions (one-line if)

age = 20
status = "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor"
print(status)

items = 3
print(f"{items} item{'s' if items != 1 else ''}")

value_if_true if condition else value_if_false: handy for choosing between two values. Use a full if statement for anything longer.

match: choosing from many patterns (Python 3.10+)

command = "stop"

match command:
    case "start":
        print("Starting…")
    case "stop" | "quit":
        print("Stopping.")
    case "help":
        print("Commands: start, stop, help")
    case _:
        print(f"Unknown command: {command}")
  • case "stop" | "quit" matches either value.
  • case _ matches anything else (like else).
  • No break needed; only one case runs.

match can also unpack structures:

point = (0, 5)

match point:
    case (0, 0):
        print("Origin")
    case (0, y):
        print(f"On the y-axis at {y}")
    case (x, 0):
        print(f"On the x-axis at {x}")
    case (x, y):
        print(f"At {x}, {y}")

For simple value checks, if/elif is often clearer; match shines with many fixed options or structured data.

A practical example: shipping cost

def shipping_cost(total, is_member, city):
    if is_member:
        return 0
    if total >= 500:
        return 0
    if city in {"Pune", "Mumbai"}:
        return 30
    return 60

print(shipping_cost(350, False, "Pune"))    # 30
print(shipping_cost(350, False, "Delhi"))   # 60
print(shipping_cost(800, False, "Delhi"))   # 0
print(shipping_cost(100, True, "Delhi"))    # 0

Common mistakes

  • **= instead of ==** in a condition: if x = 5: is a SyntaxError in Python (good, it catches the bug).
  • Missing colon or wrong indentation.
  • Wrong order of elif branches.
  • **if x == "a" or "b":** is always true; write if x in ("a", "b"):.
  • **== None** instead of is None.

Exercise

  1. Ask for a number (or set one) and print whether it's positive, negative or zero.
  2. Write a BMI category checker: under 18.5, 18.5–24.9, 25–29.9, 30 and above.
  3. Given an hour (0–23), print "Good morning", "Good afternoon" or "Good evening".
  4. Check if a year is a leap year: divisible by 4, except centuries, unless divisible by 400.
  5. Write a match statement for a simple calculator that handles +, -, * and /.

Summary

  • if, elif and else run different blocks based on conditions; the first true branch wins.
  • Combine conditions with and, or and not; chain comparisons like 0 < x < 10.
  • Use in for membership, is None for None, and truthy checks for empty values.
  • Conditional expressions and match handle short choices and many fixed options.

Next, you'll repeat actions with for and while loops.
item.excerpt:encoded: Make decisions with if, elif and else, combine conditions with and, or and not, use membership and identity tests, conditional expressions, and match statements.

item.title: Python Loops
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Loops let a program repeat work: process every line in a file, every product in a list, or keep asking until the user types a valid answer. Python has two loops: for (go through a collection) and while (repeat while a condition is true).

for loops

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]

for fruit in fruits:
    print(f"I like {fruit}")

for item in collection: takes each item in turn. It works with lists, tuples, strings, sets, dictionaries, files and more.

for letter in "Hi!":
    print(letter)

prices = {"pen": 20, "bag": 899}
for item, price in prices.items():
    print(f"{item}: ₹{price}")

range(): counting

for i in range(5):
    print(i)           # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)           # 1 to 5

for i in range(10, 0, -2):
    print(i)           # 10, 8, 6, 4, 2

range(start, stop, step) produces numbers from start up to, but not including, stop. With one argument it starts at 0.

n = 7
for i in range(1, 11):
    print(f"{n} × {i} = {n * i}")

enumerate and zip

tasks = ["Write code", "Test", "Deploy"]
for number, task in enumerate(tasks, start=1):
    print(f"{number}. {task}")

names = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]
scores = [92, 78, 85]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f"{name} scored {score}")

Avoid writing for i in range(len(tasks)): and then tasks[i]. enumerate and zip are clearer and less error-prone.

Accumulating results

Many loops build up a result:

cart = [("Notebook", 120, 3), ("Pen set", 250, 1), ("USB cable", 299, 2)]

total = 0
expensive = []
for name, price, qty in cart:
    total += price * qty
    if price > 200:
        expensive.append(name)

print(f"Total: ₹{total}")              # ₹1208
print("Items over ₹200:", expensive)

while loops

while repeats as long as its condition is true. Use it when you don't know in advance how many rounds you need:

balance = 1000
years = 0

while balance < 2000:
    balance *= 1.08          # 8% interest per year
    years += 1

print(f"Doubled after {years} years: ₹{balance:,.2f}")

Make sure something in the loop changes the condition, or it will run forever. If a program gets stuck, press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop it.

Input validation with while

answers = iter(["abc", "-5", "42"])   # pretend the user types these in turn

while True:
    text = next(answers)              # in a real program: text = input("Enter a positive number: ")
    if text.isdigit() and int(text) > 0:
        number = int(text)
        break
    print(f"'{text}' is not a positive number, try again.")

print(f"Thanks! You entered {number}.")

while True with a break is a common pattern for "keep asking until the answer is valid". (iter and next here just simulate typing so the example runs on its own.)

break and continue

numbers = [4, 9, -1, 16, 25]

for n in numbers:
    if n < 0:
        print("Found a negative number, stopping.")
        break
    print(n ** 0.5)

for n in range(1, 11):
    if n % 3 == 0:
        continue        # skip multiples of 3
    print(n, end=" ")
print()
  • break leaves the loop immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of this round and starts the next one.

print(..., end=" ") prints a space instead of a new line at the end.

Loop else

A for or while loop can have an else block that runs only if the loop finished without break:

users = ["asha", "rohan", "meera"]
search = "kabir"

for user in users:
    if user == search:
        print("Found!")
        break
else:
    print(f"{search} not found.")

It's perfect for search loops: "if we never found it, do this".

Nested loops

for row in range(1, 4):
    for col in range(1, 4):
        print(row * col, end="\t")
    print()

Output:

1	2	3
2	4	6
3	6	9

The inner loop runs completely for every round of the outer loop.

Loops vs comprehensions

When a loop just builds a list, a comprehension is shorter:

prices = [120, 250, 299, 1499]

# loop
with_tax = []
for p in prices:
    with_tax.append(round(p * 1.18))

# comprehension: same result
with_tax = [round(p * 1.18) for p in prices]
print(with_tax)

And built-in functions often replace loops entirely: sum(), min(), max(), any(), all(), sorted().

Don't change a list while looping over it

numbers = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]
for n in numbers:
    if n == 2:
        numbers.remove(n)
print(numbers)   # [1, 2, 3, 4]: one 2 was skipped!

numbers = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4]
numbers = [n for n in numbers if n != 2]
print(numbers)   # [1, 3, 4]: correct

Removing items shifts the rest, so the loop skips one. Build a new list instead.

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one with range: range(1, 10) stops at 9.
  • Infinite while loops that never update their condition.
  • **for i in range(len(x))** when you only need the items.
  • Modifying a list while iterating it.
  • Indentation: a line accidentally inside (or outside) the loop.

Exercise

  1. Print the numbers 1–20, but "Fizz" for multiples of 3, "Buzz" for multiples of 5, and "FizzBuzz" for both.
  2. Sum all even numbers from 1 to 100 with a loop, then with sum(range(...)).
  3. Count the vowels in a sentence.
  4. Use a while loop to find how many years it takes ₹10,000 to reach ₹20,000 at 7% per year.
  5. Search a list of names with a for ... else loop and print a message if the name isn't found.

Summary

  • for item in collection loops over items; range() produces numbers to count with.
  • enumerate adds positions; zip walks several collections together.
  • while repeats while a condition is true; break exits, continue skips ahead.
  • A loop's else runs when no break happened; prefer comprehensions and built-ins for simple loops.

Next, you'll organise code into reusable functions.
item.excerpt:encoded: Repeat code with for and while loops, use range, enumerate and zip, control loops with break, continue and else, and avoid common loop bugs.

item.title: Python Functions
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A function is a named, reusable block of code. Functions let you write logic once and use it everywhere, give meaningful names to steps, and test pieces of a program separately. Every good Python program is built from small functions.

Defining and calling a function

def greet():
    print("Hello! Welcome to VitalStack.")

greet()
greet()
  • def starts the definition, followed by the name, brackets and a colon.
  • The indented block is the function's body.
  • greet() calls (runs) it. Defining a function doesn't run it.

Parameters and arguments

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Asha")
greet("Rohan")

name is a parameter (a placeholder); "Asha" is an argument (the actual value).

Returning values

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(3, 4)
print(result)               # 7
print(add(add(1, 2), 10))   # 13

return sends a value back to the caller and ends the function. A function without return returns None.

def describe_age(age):
    if age < 0:
        return "invalid"
    if age < 18:
        return "minor"
    return "adult"

print(describe_age(25), describe_age(12), describe_age(-1))

print vs return

def double_print(n):
    print(n * 2)       # shows it, returns None

def double_return(n):
    return n * 2       # gives it back

a = double_print(5)    # prints 10
b = double_return(5)   # prints nothing
print(a, b)            # None 10

Return values so other code can use them; print only when the job is to show something.

Returning several values

def stats(numbers):
    return min(numbers), max(numbers), sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

low, high, average = stats([72, 95, 88, 64])
print(low, high, round(average, 1))   # 64 95 79.8

Python returns a tuple, which you can unpack.

Default values

def make_tea(sugar=1, milk=True):
    return f"Tea with {sugar} sugar(s){' and milk' if milk else ''}"

print(make_tea())
print(make_tea(2))
print(make_tea(0, milk=False))

Parameters with defaults must come after those without.

Never use a mutable default like [] or {}:

def add_item(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []          # a fresh list every call
    basket.append(item)
    return basket

print(add_item("pen"))       # ['pen']
print(add_item("book"))      # ['book'], not ['pen', 'book']

A default [] is created once and shared by every call, a famous Python gotcha. Use None and create the list inside.

Keyword arguments

You can pass arguments by name, in any order:

def create_user(name, role="student", active=True):
    return {"name": name, "role": role, "active": active}

print(create_user("Asha", active=False))
print(create_user(role="teacher", name="Rohan"))

Keyword arguments make calls self-explaining: send_email(to=..., subject=..., urgent=True) is clearer than send_email(..., ..., True).

*args and **kwargs

def total(*prices):
    return sum(prices)

print(total(10, 20, 30))      # 60

def describe(**details):
    for key, value in details.items():
        print(f"{key}: {value}")

describe(name="Meera", city="Jaipur", age=24)
  • *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.
  • **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

You can also unpack into a call:

def area(width, height):
    return width * height

size = (4, 5)
print(area(*size))                     # 20
print(area(**{"width": 2, "height": 3}))  # 6

Docstrings and type hints

def price_with_tax(price: float, rate: float = 0.18) -> float:
    """Return the price including tax, rounded to 2 decimals.

    rate is a fraction: 0.18 means 18%.
    """
    return round(price * (1 + rate), 2)

print(price_with_tax(1000))
help(price_with_tax)
  • The docstring documents what the function does; help() and editors show it.
  • Type hints (price: float, -> float) document the expected types. Python doesn't enforce them, but editors and tools like mypy use them to catch mistakes. They're very common in modern code.

Scope

Variables created inside a function are local: they exist only during the call.

def calculate():
    result = 6 * 7
    return result

print(calculate())
# print(result)   # NameError: result only existed inside the function

Functions can read variables from outside, but to reassign one you'd need the global keyword, which is usually a sign of bad design. Pass values in as parameters and return results instead.

TAX = 0.18                  # a module-level constant: fine to read

def with_tax(price):
    return price * (1 + TAX)

print(with_tax(100))

Functions are objects

You can store functions in variables, put them in lists and pass them to other functions:

def shout(text):
    return text.upper() + "!"

def whisper(text):
    return text.lower() + "…"

for style in (shout, whisper):
    print(style("Hello"))

words = ["banana", "Apple", "cherry"]
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))   # pass a function as the key

Lambda: tiny anonymous functions

square = lambda n: n * n
print(square(6))   # 36

students = [("Asha", 92), ("Rohan", 78), ("Meera", 85)]
print(sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[1], reverse=True))

lambda params: expression creates a one-line function without a name. Use lambdas for short key= functions; use def for anything longer.

Writing good functions

  • One job per function, with a name that says what it does: calculate_total, is_valid_email.
  • Short: if it doesn't fit on your screen, split it.
  • Input through parameters, output through return, no hidden global changes.
  • Docstring for anything non-obvious.
def is_valid_email(email: str) -> bool:
    """Very basic email check: one @ and a dot after it."""
    if email.count("@") != 1:
        return False
    local, domain = email.split("@")
    return bool(local) and "." in domain

print(is_valid_email("asha@example.com"))  # True
print(is_valid_email("asha@example"))      # False

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to call the function (greet instead of greet()).
  • **Forgetting return**, then getting None.
  • Mutable default arguments.
  • Too many positional parameters; use keyword arguments for clarity.
  • Relying on global variables instead of parameters.

Exercise

  1. Write celsius_to_fahrenheit(c) and test it with 0, 37 and 100.
  2. Write is_even(n) returning True or False, and use it with a list comprehension to filter evens.
  3. Write average(*numbers) that returns 0 for no numbers instead of crashing.
  4. Write format_price(amount, currency="₹", decimals=2) returning a string like "₹1,499.00".
  5. Sort a list of (product, price) tuples by price with a lambda.

Summary

  • def name(params): defines a function; name(args) calls it; return gives back a value.
  • Defaults, keyword arguments, *args and **kwargs make functions flexible; avoid mutable defaults.
  • Docstrings and type hints document functions.
  • Local variables live only inside the call; functions are objects you can pass around; lambdas are one-line functions.

Next, you'll split code into modules and use Python's standard library.
item.excerpt:encoded: Define functions with def, use parameters, return values, default and keyword arguments, *args and **kwargs, type hints, docstrings, scope and lambda.

item.title: Python Modules
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
As programs grow, one long file becomes hard to manage. Modules let you split code into files and reuse it. Python also ships with a huge standard library of ready-made modules: "batteries included". Knowing what's in it saves you from reinventing the wheel.

What is a module?

Any .py file is a module. Python's own modules work the same way: math, random, datetime are just Python (or compiled) files installed with Python.

Importing

import math

print(math.sqrt(81))
print(math.pi)

import math loads the module once, and you use its contents with math.name. The prefix makes it clear where each name comes from.

Other ways to import

from math import sqrt, pi          # import specific names
print(sqrt(16), pi)

import datetime as dt              # import with a shorter alias
print(dt.date.today().year >= 2024)

from random import choice as pick  # alias a single name
print(pick(["a", "b", "c"]))

Avoid from module import *: it dumps every name into your file, making it unclear where things come from and risking name clashes.

Some aliases are universal conventions: import numpy as np, import pandas as pd.

A tour of the standard library

datetime: dates and times

from datetime import date, datetime, timedelta

today = date(2024, 5, 1)
deadline = today + timedelta(days=14)
print(deadline)                              # 2024-05-15
print((deadline - today).days)               # 14
print(deadline.strftime("%d %b %Y"))         # 15 May 2024

moment = datetime.fromisoformat("2024-05-01T14:30:00")
print(moment.hour, moment.strftime("%I:%M %p"))   # 14 02:30 PM

random, math and statistics

import statistics

marks = [72, 95, 88, 64, 88]
print(statistics.mean(marks))     # 81.4
print(statistics.median(marks))   # 88
print(statistics.mode(marks))     # 88

os and pathlib: files and folders

from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("reports")
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(folder / "summary.txt").write_text("All good.")

for path in folder.iterdir():
    print(path.name, path.suffix, path.stat().st_size, "bytes")

pathlib makes paths work the same on Windows, macOS and Linux. / joins path parts.

json: reading and writing JSON

import json

data = {"name": "Asha", "skills": ["Python", "SQL"], "active": True}
text = json.dumps(data, indent=2)
print(text)
print(json.loads(text)["skills"][0])   # Python

More in the "Working with JSON and APIs" lesson.

collections: smarter containers

from collections import Counter, defaultdict

print(Counter("mississippi").most_common(2))   # [('i', 4), ('s', 4)]

groups = defaultdict(list)
for name, city in [("Asha", "Pune"), ("Rohan", "Delhi"), ("Kabir", "Pune")]:
    groups[city].append(name)
print(dict(groups))

Other useful modules

The official documentation at docs.python.org lists them all.

Writing your own module

Create two files in the same folder.

pricing.py:

"""Helpers for prices and tax."""

GST_RATE = 0.18

def with_tax(price, rate=GST_RATE):
    return round(price * (1 + rate), 2)

def format_inr(amount):
    return f"₹{amount:,.2f}"

shop.py:

import pricing

price = pricing.with_tax(1499)
print(pricing.format_inr(price))      # ₹1,768.82

Run python shop.py. Python finds pricing.py because it's in the same folder as the script you ran. Now any other script can reuse your pricing logic.

if __name__ == "__main__"

When Python runs a file directly, it sets the special variable __name__ to "__main__". When the file is imported, __name__ is the module's name instead. This lets a file be both a reusable module and a runnable script:

def with_tax(price, rate=0.18):
    return round(price * (1 + rate), 2)

def main():
    print("Quick check:", with_tax(100))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()   # runs only when you execute this file directly, not on import

Use this pattern in every script: it keeps test code and command-line behaviour from running when someone imports your functions.

Packages: folders of modules

A package is a folder of modules, usually with an __init__.py file:

my_app/
├── main.py
└── utils/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── pricing.py
    └── dates.py

Import with dots:

from utils.pricing import with_tax
from utils import dates

Large projects (Django, pandas) are organised as packages of packages.

How Python finds modules

When you import x, Python searches, in order:

  1. The folder of the script you ran.
  2. The standard library.
  3. Installed third-party packages (from pip, next-but-one lesson).

That's why you must never name your file after a module you use: a file called random.py or json.py in your folder hides the real module, and import random loads yours instead, with confusing errors like "module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'".

Exploring a module

import math
print(dir(math)[:10])      # names inside the module
help(math.ceil)            # documentation for one function

In VS Code, hover over a name or Ctrl+click it to jump to its source.

Common mistakes

  • Naming your files math.py, random.py, email.py, json.py…
  • **from module import *.**
  • Circular imports: a.py imports b.py which imports a.py. Move shared code into a third module.
  • **Forgetting if __name__ == "__main__":**, so importing a file runs its script code.

Exercise

  1. Use datetime to print how many days are left until 31 December of this year.
  2. Use statistics to find the mean and median of 10 numbers.
  3. Create a module textutils.py with word_count(text) and reverse_words(text), and use it from another file.
  4. Add a main() function with the __name__ check to your module and test both running and importing it.
  5. Use Counter to find the three most common words in a paragraph.

Summary

  • Every .py file is a module; import reuses its code.
  • from x import y and import x as alias control naming; avoid import *.
  • The standard library covers dates, files, JSON, maths, randomness and much more.
  • Use if __name__ == "__main__": for script code, and organise big projects into packages.

Next, you'll read and write files.
item.excerpt:encoded: Import modules, explore the standard library, write your own modules, understand if __name__ == "__main__", and organise code into packages.

item.title: Python Files
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Programs often need to keep data after they stop: logs, settings, reports, exported spreadsheets. Python makes reading and writing files simple. In this lesson you'll work with text files and CSV files, the format every spreadsheet program understands.

Writing a file

with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("First line\n")
    f.write("Second line\n")

print("Saved.")
  • open(filename, mode) opens a file and returns a file object.
  • Mode "w" means write: it creates the file, or erases it if it already exists.
  • \n adds a line break; write doesn't add one for you.
  • encoding="utf-8" makes sure all characters (₹, é, Hindi, emoji) are saved correctly on every operating system.

Why with?

with automatically closes the file when the block ends, even if an error happens. An unclosed file may not have all its data saved, and the operating system can run out of file handles. Always use with for files.

Reading a file

with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("First line\nSecond line\nThird line\n")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    content = f.read()           # the whole file as one string

print(content)

Mode "r" (read) is the default.

Line by line

For big files, read one line at a time instead of loading everything into memory:

with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("apple\nbanana\n\ncherry\n")

with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
        line = line.strip()          # remove the \n at the end
        if not line:
            continue                 # skip empty lines
        print(number, line)

Each line includes its \n, so .strip() it. You can also get a list of lines with f.read().splitlines().

Appending

Mode "a" adds to the end of the file without erasing it. Perfect for logs:

from datetime import datetime

def log(message):
    with open("app.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(f"{datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S} {message}\n")

log("App started")
log("User signed in")

with open("app.log", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())

File modes

Be careful with "w": opening an existing file in write mode deletes its contents immediately.

Handling missing files

try:
    with open("does_not_exist.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        print(f.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found. Check the name and folder.")

You'll learn try/except fully in the next lesson.

pathlib: the modern way to handle paths

from pathlib import Path

reports = Path("reports")
reports.mkdir(exist_ok=True)               # create the folder if needed

file = reports / "summary.txt"             # join paths with /
file.write_text("Sales: ₹12,400\n", encoding="utf-8")
print(file.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

print(file.exists(), file.name, file.stem, file.suffix)
print(file.resolve())                       # the full absolute path

for txt in reports.glob("*.txt"):           # find files by pattern
    print("Found:", txt)

Path works on Windows, macOS and Linux without worrying about \ vs /. For small files, read_text and write_text are a one-line alternative to open.

Where is the file?

Relative paths like "notes.txt" are relative to the current working directory: the folder you ran Python from, which isn't always where the script lives. To use files next to your script:

from pathlib import Path
HERE = Path(__file__).parent
data_file = HERE / "data.txt"

CSV files

CSV (comma-separated values) is the simplest spreadsheet format. Excel and Google Sheets can open and save it. Use the csv module rather than splitting on commas yourself, because values can contain commas inside quotes.

Writing CSV

import csv

products = [
    {"name": "Notebook", "price": 120, "stock": 50},
    {"name": "Pen set", "price": 250, "stock": 30},
    {"name": "Backpack, large", "price": 1899, "stock": 12},
]

with open("products.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["name", "price", "stock"])
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(products)

print(open("products.csv", encoding="utf-8").read())

Note newline="", which the csv module needs to avoid blank lines on Windows. "Backpack, large" is automatically quoted because it contains a comma.

Reading CSV

import csv

with open("products.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("name,price,stock\nNotebook,120,50\nPen set,250,30\n\"Backpack, large\",1899,12\n")

with open("products.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    total_value = 0
    for row in reader:
        value = int(row["price"]) * int(row["stock"])
        total_value += value
        print(f"{row['name']:<16} ₹{value:>7,}")

print(f"Inventory value: ₹{total_value:,}")

DictReader gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the header row. All values are strings, so convert numbers with int() or float().

Reading files in other encodings

If you get a UnicodeDecodeError, the file was saved with a different encoding. Files from older Windows programs are often "cp1252"; Excel's "CSV UTF-8" format uses "utf-8-sig". Try open(name, encoding="utf-8-sig").

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting with**, leaving files open.
  • **Using "w" when you meant "a"**, erasing data.
  • **Forgetting \n** when writing lines.
  • Not stripping lines when reading, leaving \n in your data.
  • Treating CSV values as numbers without converting.
  • Wrong working directory, so the file "isn't found" even though it exists.

Exercise

  1. Write a program that saves five of your favourite films to films.txt, one per line, then reads them back with numbers.
  2. Add a "journal" function that appends today's date and a message to journal.txt.
  3. Count the lines, words and characters in a text file.
  4. Write a CSV of three students with name and score, then read it and print the average score.
  5. Use pathlib to list every .txt file in a folder with its size.

Summary

  • with open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") as f: opens files safely; they close automatically.
  • "r" reads, "w" overwrites, "a" appends; loop over a file to read line by line.
  • pathlib.Path builds paths and reads/writes small files easily.
  • The csv module (DictReader, DictWriter) handles spreadsheets correctly; convert values from strings.

Next, you'll handle errors gracefully with try and except.
item.excerpt:encoded: Read and write text files safely with open() and with, process files line by line, append data, work with CSV files, and handle paths with pathlib.

item.title: Python Errors and Exceptions
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Things go wrong: users type letters where numbers belong, files go missing, networks drop. When Python hits a problem it can't handle, it raises an exception and stops the program. With try and except, you can catch exceptions and respond sensibly instead of crashing.

Syntax errors vs exceptions

  • A syntax error means the code isn't valid Python (missing colon, unclosed bracket). The program doesn't start at all. You fix these by correcting the code.
  • An exception happens while the program runs: the code is valid, but something fails at that moment.
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
# print(numbers[10])   # IndexError: list index out of range
# int("abc")           # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
# 10 / 0               # ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
# {"a": 1}["b"]        # KeyError: 'b'
# "age" + 5            # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
print("Each commented line above would raise a different exception.")

try and except

text = "abc"

try:
    number = int(text)
    print(f"You entered {number}")
except ValueError:
    print(f"'{text}' is not a whole number.")

print("The program keeps running.")
  • Code that might fail goes in try.
  • If an exception of the named type happens, Python jumps to the matching except block.
  • If nothing fails, the except block is skipped.

Catch specific exceptions

def safe_divide(a, b):
    try:
        return a / b
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print("Can't divide by zero.")
        return None
    except TypeError:
        print("Both values must be numbers.")
        return None

print(safe_divide(10, 2))
print(safe_divide(10, 0))
print(safe_divide(10, "2"))

Several except blocks handle different problems differently. You can also catch several types in one block: except (ValueError, TypeError):.

Don't catch everything blindly

# Avoid:
try:
    result = 10 / 0
except:                # catches EVERYTHING, even Ctrl+C and typos in your own code
    print("Something went wrong")

A bare except: (or except Exception: used carelessly) hides real bugs: a misspelled variable becomes "something went wrong" with no clue why. Catch the specific exceptions you expect and know how to handle.

Getting the error message

try:
    value = int("12.5")
except ValueError as error:
    print("Problem:", error)
    print("Type:", type(error).__name__)

as error gives you the exception object, whose text explains the problem. It's useful for logging.

else and finally

def read_number(text):
    try:
        number = float(text)
    except ValueError:
        print(f"Invalid: {text!r}")
    else:
        print(f"Valid number: {number}")     # runs only if no exception
    finally:
        print("Check complete.")             # always runs

read_number("3.14")
read_number("pi")
  • else runs only when the try block succeeded. Keep the try block small and put the follow-up code in else, so you don't accidentally catch errors from it.
  • finally always runs, error or not. It's for clean-up: closing connections, deleting temporary files, stopping a timer. (with blocks do this automatically for files.)

A real pattern: retrying user input

attempts = iter(["twelve", "-3", "12"])   # simulated user input

while True:
    raw = next(attempts)                   # in a real program: raw = input("Quantity: ")
    try:
        quantity = int(raw)
        if quantity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("must be positive")
    except ValueError as error:
        print(f"'{raw}' isn't valid ({error}). Try again.")
    else:
        break

print(f"Ordering {quantity} items.")

Raising exceptions

Your own functions should raise exceptions when they receive bad input, rather than returning wrong results silently:

def withdraw(balance, amount):
    if amount <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Amount must be positive.")
    if amount > balance:
        raise ValueError(f"Insufficient funds: balance is {balance}.")
    return balance - amount

print(withdraw(1000, 300))

try:
    withdraw(1000, 5000)
except ValueError as error:
    print("Error:", error)

raise ExceptionType("message") stops the function and passes the problem to the caller, who decides what to do (show a message, retry, log it). This separates detecting a problem from handling it.

Custom exceptions

For bigger programs, define your own exception types so callers can catch exactly your errors:

class InsufficientFundsError(Exception):
    """Raised when a withdrawal is larger than the balance."""

class Account:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise InsufficientFundsError(f"Need {amount}, have {self.balance}")
        self.balance -= amount

account = Account(500)
try:
    account.withdraw(800)
except InsufficientFundsError as error:
    print("Declined:", error)

You'll learn classes properly in the next lesson; a custom exception just needs class Name(Exception):.

EAFP: Python's style

Python code often follows "Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission": try the operation and handle the exception, instead of checking everything first.

settings = {"theme": "dark"}

# Look before you leap (LBYL)
if "font_size" in settings:
    size = settings["font_size"]
else:
    size = 16

# EAFP
try:
    size = settings["font_size"]
except KeyError:
    size = 16

print(size)

Both are fine; here settings.get("font_size", 16) is shortest of all. EAFP is especially useful for files and networks, where the situation can change between checking and acting.

Reading tracebacks

When an exception isn't caught, Python prints a traceback:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "shop.py", line 12, in <module>
    total = checkout(cart)
  File "shop.py", line 7, in checkout
    return sum(item["price"] for item in cart)
  File "shop.py", line 7, in <genexpr>
    return sum(item["price"] for item in cart)
KeyError: 'price'

Read it bottom-up: the last line is the error (KeyError: 'price', an item without a price). Above it is the chain of calls, ending with the exact line that failed. Look at the deepest line in your code first.

Common exception types

Common mistakes

  • **Bare except:** that hides bugs.
  • **Huge try blocks** that catch errors from unrelated lines.
  • Silently ignoring errors (except: pass), so problems go unnoticed.
  • Returning error codes like -1 instead of raising exceptions.

Exercise

  1. Write to_int(text) that returns an int, or None with a printed message if conversion fails.
  2. Write get_item(items, index) that returns the item or "not found" using try/except IndexError.
  3. Read a file name from a variable and print its contents, with a friendly message if it doesn't exist.
  4. Write set_age(age) that raises ValueError for ages below 0 or above 130, and call it inside try.
  5. Create a custom OutOfStockError and raise it from a buy(product, qty) function.

Summary

  • Exceptions are runtime errors; try/except catches them so your program can respond.
  • Catch specific exception types; use as error to read the message.
  • else runs on success; finally always runs for clean-up.
  • raise signals problems in your own functions; custom exceptions make errors precise.

Next, you'll model real-world things with classes and objects.
item.excerpt:encoded: Handle errors with try, except, else and finally, catch specific exceptions, raise your own, create custom exception classes, and read tracebacks.

item.title: Python Classes and Objects
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
So far you've used Python's built-in types: strings, lists, dictionaries. Classes let you create your own types that bundle data and behaviour together: a BankAccount with a balance and a deposit() method, a Product with a price and a discounted() method. This style is called object-oriented programming (OOP).

Class and object

  • A class is a blueprint: it describes what data and abilities something has.
  • An object (or instance) is one thing built from that blueprint.

You've already used objects: "hello" is an object of class str, and .upper() is one of its methods.

Defining a class

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says woof!"

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
bella = Dog("Bella", 5)

print(rex.name, rex.age)    # Rex 3
print(bella.bark())         # Bella says woof!
  • class Dog: defines the class. Class names use PascalCase.
  • __init__ is the initialiser: it runs automatically when you create an object and sets up its data.
  • self is the object being created or used. self.name = name stores the value on that object.
  • bark is a method: a function that belongs to the class. Its first parameter is always self.
  • Dog("Rex", 3) creates an object; Python passes the new object as self automatically.

Each object has its own data: changing rex.age doesn't affect bella.

A more useful example: a bank account

class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance
        self.history = []

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Deposit must be positive.")
        self.balance += amount
        self.history.append(("deposit", amount))

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds.")
        self.balance -= amount
        self.history.append(("withdraw", amount))

account = BankAccount("Asha", 1000)
account.deposit(500)
account.withdraw(200)
print(account.balance)      # 1300
print(account.history)      # [('deposit', 500), ('withdraw', 200)]

The object keeps its own state (balance, history), and the methods are the only intended way to change it, with rules built in. That's the main benefit of classes: data and the rules for changing it live together.

Class attributes

Attributes defined directly in the class are shared by all objects:

class Product:
    tax_rate = 0.18             # class attribute: same for every product

    def __init__(self, name, price):
        self.name = name        # instance attributes: different per product
        self.price = price

    def price_with_tax(self):
        return round(self.price * (1 + Product.tax_rate), 2)

pen = Product("Pen set", 250)
bag = Product("Backpack", 1899)
print(pen.price_with_tax(), bag.price_with_tax())   # 295.0 2240.82

Use class attributes for constants and settings shared by all instances. Don't use a mutable class attribute (like a list) for per-object data: every object would share the same list.

Special methods: __str__ and __repr__

Printing an object normally shows something unhelpful like <__main__.Product object at 0x7f…>. Special methods (with double underscores, "dunder" methods) customise built-in behaviour:

class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, price):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.name} (₹{self.price:,})"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Product({self.name!r}, {self.price})"

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return isinstance(other, Product) and (self.name, self.price) == (other.name, other.price)

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.price < other.price

items = [Product("Backpack", 1899), Product("Notebook", 120), Product("Pen set", 250)]
print(items[0])                     # Backpack (₹1,899)
print(items)                        # uses __repr__ for items inside a list
print(sorted(items))                # sorting works thanks to __lt__
print(Product("A", 1) == Product("A", 1))   # True thanks to __eq__
  • __str__: friendly text for print() and str().
  • __repr__: unambiguous text for developers, shown in lists and the REPL.
  • __eq__, __lt__: make == and sorting work.
  • Others include __len__ (for len()), __add__ (for +) and __contains__ (for in).

Properties: computed and protected attributes

class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self.celsius = celsius

    @property
    def fahrenheit(self):
        return self.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32

    @property
    def celsius(self):
        return self._celsius

    @celsius.setter
    def celsius(self, value):
        if value < -273.15:
            raise ValueError("Below absolute zero!")
        self._celsius = value

t = Temperature(25)
print(t.fahrenheit)     # 77.0: computed, used like an attribute
t.celsius = 30          # goes through the setter's check
print(t.fahrenheit)     # 86.0

@property turns a method into something you read like an attribute. A setter adds validation. A leading underscore (_celsius) is a convention meaning "internal: don't touch from outside". Python doesn't enforce privacy; it trusts developers to respect the convention.

Inheritance

A class can inherit from another, reusing its code and adding or changing behaviour:

class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds.")
        self.balance -= amount

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: ₹{self.balance:,}"

class SavingsAccount(Account):
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, rate=0.04):
        super().__init__(owner, balance)     # run the parent's __init__
        self.rate = rate

    def add_interest(self):
        self.balance += round(self.balance * self.rate)

    def describe(self):                       # override the parent method
        return super().describe() + f" (savings, {self.rate:.0%})"

s = SavingsAccount("Meera", 10000)
s.add_interest()
s.withdraw(400)                               # inherited method
print(s.describe())                           # Meera: ₹10,000 (savings, 4%)
print(isinstance(s, Account))                 # True
  • class SavingsAccount(Account): inherits everything from Account.
  • super() calls the parent's version of a method.
  • Defining a method with the same name overrides the parent's.

Use inheritance for genuine "is a" relationships (a savings account is an account). For "has a" relationships (a car has an engine), store one object inside another instead; this is called composition and is often simpler.

Dataclasses: less boilerplate

For classes that mainly hold data, dataclass writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Expense:
    title: str
    amount: float
    category: str = "other"
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def is_large(self):
        return self.amount > 1000

e = Expense("Groceries", 1450.5, "food")
print(e)                 # Expense(title='Groceries', amount=1450.5, category='food', tags=[])
print(e.is_large())      # True
print(e == Expense("Groceries", 1450.5, "food"))   # True

field(default_factory=list) gives each object its own new list (the safe way to have a mutable default). Dataclasses are used a lot in modern Python, and you'll use one in the project lesson.

When to use classes

Use a class when you have data and behaviour that belong together, or you need many objects of the same kind with their own state. For a simple calculation, a function is enough; for simple records, a dictionary or dataclass often is.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting self** as the first method parameter, or forgetting self. when using attributes (balance += 1 instead of self.balance += 1).
  • Calling the method on the class instead of an object: Dog.bark().
  • Mutable class attributes shared by accident.
  • Deep inheritance trees; prefer composition and keep hierarchies shallow.

Exercise

  1. Create a Book class with title, author and pages, and a __str__ like "Title by Author (300 pages)".
  2. Add a method is_long() that returns True for books over 400 pages.
  3. Create a Rectangle class with area and perimeter properties.
  4. Create a Student class with a list of marks and methods add_mark(mark) and average().
  5. Create Shape with area() returning 0, and Circle and Square subclasses that override it. Put several shapes in a list and print their areas.

Summary

  • A class is a blueprint; objects are instances with their own data.
  • __init__ sets up attributes on self; methods are functions that take self.
  • Special methods like __str__, __eq__ and __lt__ hook into Python's built-in behaviour.
  • Properties compute or validate attributes; inheritance reuses and extends classes; dataclasses remove boilerplate.

Next, you'll install third-party packages with pip and manage them with virtual environments.
item.excerpt:encoded: Object-oriented programming in Python: define classes, create objects, use __init__, attributes and methods, class attributes, special methods, properties, inheritance and dataclasses.

item.title: Python pip and Packages
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Python's standard library is big, but the real superpower is the ecosystem: over half a million free packages on PyPI (the Python Package Index) for web apps, data analysis, AI, automation and more. pip is the tool that installs them. In this lesson you'll install packages the professional way, inside virtual environments.

What is a package?

A package is code someone else wrote and published so you can use it with import. Examples:

Step 1: Create a virtual environment

If you install every package into your main Python, different projects soon need different versions of the same package and break each other. A virtual environment (venv) is a private folder of packages for one project.

In your project folder:

python -m venv .venv

This creates a .venv folder containing a copy of Python and an empty set of packages. (Use python3 on macOS and Linux.)

Step 2: Activate it

# Windows (Command Prompt or PowerShell)
.venv\Scripts\activate

# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate

Your prompt now starts with (.venv). While it's active, python and pip refer to the environment's versions, and packages install into .venv only. Type deactivate to leave.

VS Code detects .venv automatically and offers to use it; if not, press Ctrl+Shift+P → Python: Select Interpreter and choose the .venv one.

(On Windows PowerShell, if activation is blocked, run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned once.)

Step 3: Install packages

pip install requests

pip downloads requests and everything it depends on from PyPI. Then use it in your code:

import requests

response = requests.get("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1", timeout=10)
print(response.status_code)
print(response.json()["title"])

Useful pip commands

pip install requests pandas      # install several
pip install "requests==2.32.3"   # an exact version
pip install --upgrade requests   # upgrade to the latest
pip uninstall requests           # remove
