Only the desk lamp has never sold. Maybe it needs a better photo or a lower price.

Counting with zeros

INNER JOIN reports leave out the zeros. LEFT JOIN includes them:

SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name;

Important: use COUNT(o.id), not COUNT(*). For Sara there's still one row (with NULLs), so COUNT(*) would say 1. COUNT(o.id) counts only non-NULL order ids, giving the correct 0.

Sums with COALESCE

SELECT p.name,
       COALESCE(SUM(oi.qty), 0) AS units_sold
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY units_sold DESC;

The desk lamp shows 0 instead of NULL, because SUM of nothing is NULL and COALESCE turns it into 0.

WHERE vs ON with LEFT JOIN

This is the trickiest part of LEFT JOIN. Compare:

-- A: condition in WHERE
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered';
-- B: condition in ON
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'delivered';
  • A returns only Rohan, Asha and Kabir with their delivered orders. The WHERE runs after the join and removes rows where o.status is NULL, so Sara and Meera disappear: the LEFT JOIN has effectively become an INNER JOIN.
  • B returns all five customers: those with a delivered order show it; Meera and Sara show NULLs.

Rule: conditions on the right table go in ON if you want to keep all left rows. Conditions on the left table go in WHERE.

Order of tables matters

A LEFT JOIN B keeps all of A. B LEFT JOIN A keeps all of B. Start FROM the table whose rows you want to keep completely.

RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN

-- RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows of the right table:
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM orders o
RIGHT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id;
-- Same result as: customers LEFT JOIN orders

RIGHT JOIN is just a LEFT JOIN written backwards. Most developers always use LEFT JOIN and order the tables accordingly; it's easier to read. (SQLite added RIGHT JOIN in version 3.39.)

FULL OUTER JOIN keeps all rows from both tables, with NULLs on either side where there's no match. It's supported by PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite 3.39+, but not MySQL. It's mostly used for comparing two lists, e.g. reconciling two systems.

Self join

A table can be joined to itself with two aliases. For example, customers from the same city:

SELECT a.name AS customer, b.name AS neighbour, a.city
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON a.city = b.city AND a.id < b.id;

Asha and Kabir (both Pune). a.id < b.id avoids pairing someone with themselves and listing each pair twice. Self joins are also used for hierarchies, like an employees table where manager_id points to another employee.

Join types at a glance

Common mistakes

  • Filtering the right table in WHERE, which silently turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
  • **COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(right.id)**, giving 1 instead of 0.
  • Forgetting COALESCE, showing NULL instead of 0 in reports.
  • Putting the "keep all" table on the wrong side.

Exercise

  1. List all products with the total quantity sold, including 0 for unsold products.
  2. Find customers who have never ordered.
  3. Show every customer with the number of delivered orders (0 if none). Hint: put the status condition in ON.
  4. List every order with the number of items in it, including orders with no items. (Insert an empty order first to test.)
  5. Find pairs of products in the same category with a self join.

Summary

  • LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills missing matches with NULL.
  • WHERE right.id IS NULL finds rows without a match.
  • Use COUNT(right.id) and COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) for correct zeros.
  • Conditions on the right table belong in ON to keep all left rows.

Next, you'll protect your data with constraints and keys.
item.excerpt:encoded: Keep every row from the first table with LEFT JOIN, find rows without matches, count zero values correctly, and meet RIGHT, FULL and self joins.

item.title: SQL Constraints and Keys
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Application code has bugs, users type strange things, and scripts get run twice. Constraints are rules the database itself enforces, so bad data can't get in no matter where it comes from. They're your last and strongest line of defence for data quality.

The constraints

A table with every constraint

CREATE TABLE reviews (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  rating      INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  comment     TEXT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  UNIQUE (product_id, customer_id)
);

Read it rule by rule:

  • Every review has a unique id.
  • It must point to a real product and a real customer.
  • The rating is required and must be 1–5.
  • The comment is optional.
  • created_at fills itself in.
  • A customer can review each product only once (the pair must be unique).
  • If a product is deleted, its reviews are deleted with it.

Testing the rules

Turn on foreign keys if you're using SQLite, then try some inserts:

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;  -- SQLite only

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id, rating, comment)
VALUES (1, 1, 5, 'Great paper quality');           -- OK

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id, rating)
VALUES (1, 2, 7);                                  -- CHECK fails: rating must be 1–5

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id, rating)
VALUES (1, 1, 4);                                  -- UNIQUE fails: Asha already reviewed product 1

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id, rating)
VALUES (99, 1, 4);                                 -- FOREIGN KEY fails: no product 99

INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, customer_id)
VALUES (2, 1);                                     -- NOT NULL fails: rating is required

Each bad insert is rejected with an error explaining which rule failed. Your application can catch these errors and show a friendly message.

Primary keys

  • Exactly one per table; values unique and never NULL.
  • Usually a meaningless number (id) generated by the database. Don't use real-world values like email or phone as primary keys: people change them.
  • A composite primary key uses several columns, like PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id) in order_items: each product appears at most once per order.

Foreign keys

A foreign key links a column to the primary key of another table:

-- customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(id)
-- or, as a separate line:
-- FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)

It guarantees referential integrity: every order belongs to a customer who exists. Without it, deleting customers would leave orphaned orders pointing at nothing.

ON DELETE options

Choose per relationship:

  • Reviews of a deleted product → CASCADE (they're meaningless alone).
  • Orders of a deleted customer → RESTRICT (keep financial records; deactivate the customer instead).
  • Posts by a deleted author → SET NULL (keep the posts, show "former author").

There's also ON UPDATE CASCADE, rarely needed when ids never change.

UNIQUE

-- email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE

Guarantees no duplicates, e.g. one account per email. It's much safer than checking in application code ("is this email taken?") because two sign-ups at the same instant could both pass the check. The database never lets both through.

Most databases allow several NULLs in a UNIQUE column, since NULL means "unknown". That's why Sara (no email) doesn't conflict with anyone.

CHECK

-- price DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (price >= 0)
-- status VARCHAR(20) CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled'))
-- CHECK (end_date >= start_date)

Any condition on the row's own values. (MySQL enforces CHECK from version 8.0.16; older versions ignored it.)

Adding constraints to existing tables

-- MySQL / PostgreSQL:
-- ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT price_positive CHECK (price >= 0);
-- ALTER TABLE customers ADD CONSTRAINT email_unique UNIQUE (email);

Adding a constraint fails if existing data already breaks it, so clean the data first. (SQLite has limited ALTER TABLE support; there you usually recreate the table.) Naming constraints makes error messages clearer.

Relationship design

One-to-many

One customer → many orders. Put the foreign key on the "many" side: orders.customer_id.

Many-to-many

One order has many products; one product appears in many orders. You need a junction table in between: order_items(order_id, product_id, qty), with two foreign keys and a composite primary key. Other examples: students ↔ courses (enrollments), posts ↔ tags (post_tags).

CREATE TABLE tags (
  id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE product_tags (
  product_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tag_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES tags(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  PRIMARY KEY (product_id, tag_id)
);

One-to-one

One user ↔ one profile. Use a foreign key that's also UNIQUE (or the primary key itself). Often it's simpler to keep the columns in one table.

Common mistakes

  • No foreign keys "for speed", then years of orphaned and inconsistent data.
  • Natural keys (email, phone) as primary keys.
  • Duplicate checks only in code, instead of UNIQUE.
  • CASCADE everywhere, so one mistaken delete wipes related history.
  • **Forgetting PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON** in SQLite.

Exercise

  1. Create the reviews table and test each failing insert above.
  2. Add a CHECK so product stock can never be negative (on a new test table).
  3. Design tables for students, courses and enrollments (with an enrollment date), including all keys.
  4. Decide the ON DELETE behaviour for: comments when a post is deleted; invoices when a customer is deleted. Explain why.

Summary

  • Constraints make the database enforce data rules: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT.
  • Foreign keys keep relationships valid; ON DELETE decides what happens to children.
  • UNIQUE is the reliable way to prevent duplicates.
  • One-to-many uses a foreign key; many-to-many uses a junction table.

Next, you'll make queries fast with indexes.
item.excerpt:encoded: Protect data quality with PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints, choose ON DELETE behaviour, and design one-to-many and many-to-many relationships.

item.title: SQL Indexes
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
With 7 products, every query is instant. With 7 million, a query that scans every row can take seconds, and a busy website runs thousands of queries a minute. Indexes let the database find rows without reading the whole table. They're the single biggest tool for database performance.

The book index analogy

To find "foreign keys" in a 500-page book, you don't read every page. You check the index at the back: "foreign keys … page 312". A database index works the same way: a separate, sorted structure that maps column values to the rows that contain them.

Without an index, the database does a full table scan: it checks every row. With one, it jumps almost straight to the matches, even in a table with millions of rows.

Creating an index

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
  • idx_orders_customer_id is the index's name (a common convention: idx_table_column).
  • ON orders (customer_id) says which table and column.

Queries filtering, joining or sorting on customer_id can now use it:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;

You don't change your queries; the database decides automatically when an index helps.

Indexes you already have

  • Every PRIMARY KEY is indexed automatically.
  • Every UNIQUE constraint creates an index (that's how the database checks uniqueness quickly).
  • Foreign keys are indexed automatically in MySQL (InnoDB), but not in PostgreSQL or SQLite. Index them yourself there, because joins use them constantly.

Seeing the query plan with EXPLAIN

EXPLAIN shows how the database will run a query:

-- SQLite:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';
-- SCAN orders                      ← full table scan

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders (status);

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';
-- SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_status (status=?)   ← uses the index

In MySQL and PostgreSQL, write EXPLAIN SELECT …. Look for "full scan" / "Seq Scan" / "type: ALL" on big tables: that's where indexes help. PostgreSQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and shows real timings.

(On tiny tables, databases often choose a scan anyway, because it's faster than using the index.)

What to index

Index columns that appear often in:

  • WHERE filters: WHERE email = ?, WHERE status = ?.
  • JOIN conditions: foreign keys like orders.customer_id, order_items.product_id.
  • ORDER BY: ORDER BY created_at DESC on large tables (latest posts, newest orders).

Start from real slow queries. Most databases can log slow queries (MySQL's slow query log, PostgreSQL's pg_stat_statements).

Composite indexes and column order

An index can cover several columns:

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date ON orders (customer_id, order_date);

It's sorted by customer_id first, then by order_date within each customer, like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name. It helps:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;                                -- yes (first column)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 AND order_date >= '2024-05-05'; -- yes, both columns
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY order_date DESC;       -- yes, even the sort
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2024-05-05';                     -- no (not the first column)

This is the leftmost prefix rule: an index can be used for its first column, or first two, and so on, but not for a later column on its own. Put the column used for equality (=) first and range or sort columns after it.

When indexes can't be used

-- Function on the column: the index on email can't be used
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE LOWER(email) = 'asha@example.com';

-- Leading wildcard: like searching a phone book for names ending in "-sharma"
SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%lamp';

-- These CAN use an index:
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = 'asha@example.com';
SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'Desk%';

Store data in a consistent form (e.g. emails lower-cased on insert) so you can compare directly. PostgreSQL and MySQL 8 also support expression indexes, such as an index on LOWER(email). For searching words inside text, use full-text search.

Unique indexes

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_customers_email ON customers (email);

An index that also enforces uniqueness, the same as a UNIQUE constraint.

The cost of indexes

Indexes aren't free:

  • Slower writes: every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update every index on the table.
  • Disk space: each index is a copy of its columns, sorted.
  • Maintenance: unused indexes still cost on every write.

So don't index every column. Index what your queries actually need, and remove indexes nobody uses.

Indexes in WordPress

WordPress's wp_posts table has indexes on post_name (slug lookups), on (post_type, post_status, post_date, ID) for listing posts, and on post_author. That's why loading a post by its URL stays fast even with thousands of posts. Plugins that search unindexed meta values (wp_postmeta.meta_value) are a common cause of slow WordPress sites.

Removing an index

DROP INDEX idx_orders_status;              -- SQLite / PostgreSQL
-- DROP INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders; -- MySQL

Common mistakes

  • No index on foreign keys in PostgreSQL/SQLite, making joins slow.
  • Indexing everything, slowing down every write.
  • Wrong column order in composite indexes.
  • Wrapping indexed columns in functions in WHERE.
  • Guessing instead of measuring with EXPLAIN.

Exercise

  1. Run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN (SQLite) or EXPLAIN on SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE product_id = 1. Then create an index and compare.
  2. Create a composite index on orders (status, order_date). Which of these could use it: filter by status; by status and date; by date only?
  3. List the indexes you'd add to the shop database, and explain each one.
  4. Rewrite WHERE LOWER(city) = 'pune' so it could use an index on city.

Summary

  • Indexes are sorted lookup structures that avoid full table scans.
  • Primary keys and UNIQUE columns are indexed automatically; index foreign keys yourself where needed.
  • Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix rule; order the columns carefully.
  • Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes; measure with EXPLAIN.

Next, you'll design and query a complete library database in the SQL project.
item.excerpt:encoded: How indexes make queries fast, when to create them, composite indexes and column order, reading EXPLAIN plans, and the costs of too many indexes.

item.title: SQL Project: Library Database
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Time to put the whole course together. You'll design a database for a small library, create it with constraints, load sample data, and answer real questions a librarian would ask, from "which books are overdue?" to "who are our most active readers?".

Run everything in sqliteonline.com, DB Browser for SQLite or any SQLite tool. (Small changes for MySQL and PostgreSQL are noted.)

Step 1: Design

What does a library need to track?

  • Authors: name, country.
  • Books: title, year, genre, number of copies. Each book has one author (we'll keep it simple).
  • Members: name, email, join date.
  • Loans: which member borrowed which book, when, when it's due, and when it came back.

Relationships:

authors 1 ──< books 1 ──< loans >── 1 members

One author writes many books. One book can be loaned many times; one member can borrow many books. loans connects books and members, and also stores details about each borrowing.

Step 2: Create the tables

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

CREATE TABLE authors (
  id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  country  VARCHAR(50)
);

CREATE TABLE books (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title      VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  author_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES authors(id),
  genre      VARCHAR(50),
  year       INTEGER CHECK (year > 0),
  copies     INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (copies >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE members (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name    VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  email   VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  joined  DATE NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE loans (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  book_id      INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES books(id),
  member_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES members(id),
  loaned_on    DATE NOT NULL,
  due_on       DATE NOT NULL,
  returned_on  DATE,
  CHECK (due_on >= loaned_on)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_books_author ON books (author_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_loans_book ON loans (book_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_loans_member ON loans (member_id);

Design decisions:

  • returned_on is NULL while a book is still out. That single column tells us the loan's status.
  • CHECK constraints stop impossible data (negative copies, due before loaned).
  • Foreign key columns are indexed for fast joins.

Step 3: Load sample data

INSERT INTO authors (id, name, country) VALUES
  (1, 'R. K. Narayan', 'India'),
  (2, 'Agatha Christie', 'UK'),
  (3, 'Paulo Coelho', 'Brazil'),
  (4, 'Ruskin Bond', 'India'),
  (5, 'Yuval Noah Harari', 'Israel');

INSERT INTO books (id, title, author_id, genre, year, copies) VALUES
  (1, 'Malgudi Days', 1, 'fiction', 1943, 3),
  (2, 'The Guide', 1, 'fiction', 1958, 2),
  (3, 'Murder on the Orient Express', 2, 'mystery', 1934, 2),
  (4, 'And Then There Were None', 2, 'mystery', 1939, 1),
  (5, 'The Alchemist', 3, 'fiction', 1988, 4),
  (6, 'The Blue Umbrella', 4, 'children', 1980, 2),
  (7, 'Sapiens', 5, 'history', 2011, 3);

INSERT INTO members (id, name, email, joined) VALUES
  (1, 'Asha', 'asha@example.com', '2024-01-05'),
  (2, 'Rohan', 'rohan@example.com', '2024-02-11'),
  (3, 'Meera', 'meera@example.com', '2024-03-02'),
  (4, 'Kabir', 'kabir@example.com', '2024-04-18');

INSERT INTO loans (id, book_id, member_id, loaned_on, due_on, returned_on) VALUES
  (1, 1, 1, '2024-05-01', '2024-05-15', '2024-05-12'),
  (2, 3, 1, '2024-05-14', '2024-05-28', NULL),
  (3, 5, 2, '2024-05-03', '2024-05-17', '2024-05-20'),
  (4, 7, 2, '2024-05-21', '2024-06-04', NULL),
  (5, 5, 3, '2024-05-10', '2024-05-24', '2024-05-22'),
  (6, 6, 3, '2024-06-01', '2024-06-15', NULL),
  (7, 1, 1, '2024-06-02', '2024-06-16', NULL),
  (8, 4, 2, '2024-06-03', '2024-06-17', NULL);

Kabir has never borrowed anything, and *The Guide* has never been loaned. Those cases matter for the LEFT JOIN questions.

Step 4: Answer real questions

We'll pretend today is 2024-06-10, so results don't depend on when you run them. In a real app you'd use DATE('now') (SQLite), CURDATE() (MySQL) or CURRENT_DATE (PostgreSQL).

1. Every book with its author

SELECT b.title, a.name AS author, b.year
FROM books b
JOIN authors a ON a.id = b.author_id
ORDER BY a.name, b.year;

2. Books currently on loan, and who has them

SELECT b.title, m.name AS member, l.due_on
FROM loans l
JOIN books b   ON b.id = l.book_id
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL
ORDER BY l.due_on;

Five books are out: Murder on the Orient Express (Asha), Sapiens (Rohan), The Blue Umbrella (Meera), Malgudi Days (Asha) and And Then There Were None (Rohan).

3. Overdue loans

SELECT m.name, m.email, b.title, l.due_on
FROM loans l
JOIN books b   ON b.id = l.book_id
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
WHERE l.returned_on IS NULL
  AND l.due_on < '2024-06-10'
ORDER BY l.due_on;

Asha's *Murder on the Orient Express* (due 28 May) and Rohan's *Sapiens* (due 4 June). This is the list for reminder emails.

4. Copies available right now

SELECT b.title,
       b.copies,
       COUNT(l.id) AS on_loan,
       b.copies - COUNT(l.id) AS available
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.book_id = b.id AND l.returned_on IS NULL
GROUP BY b.id, b.title, b.copies
ORDER BY available, b.title;

The LEFT JOIN keeps books with no active loans, and the condition sits in ON so they aren't filtered out. *And Then There Were None* has 0 copies available.

5. Most popular books (all-time loans)

SELECT b.title, COUNT(l.id) AS times_borrowed
FROM books b
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.book_id = b.id
GROUP BY b.id, b.title
ORDER BY times_borrowed DESC, b.title;

*Malgudi Days* and *The Alchemist* lead with 2 loans each; *The Guide* shows 0.

6. Most active members

SELECT m.name,
       COUNT(l.id) AS loans,
       SUM(CASE WHEN l.id IS NOT NULL AND l.returned_on IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS still_out
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.member_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY loans DESC, m.name;

Asha and Rohan have 3 loans each (2 still out), Meera 2 (1 still out), Kabir 0.

Why l.id IS NOT NULL? Kabir has no loans, so the LEFT JOIN gives him one row where every loan column is NULL, including returned_on. Without the extra check, that empty row would count as "1 book still out". Whenever you test for NULL on the right side of a LEFT JOIN, ask yourself: does NULL mean "no value" or "no matching row"?

7. Members who returned a book late

SELECT DISTINCT m.name
FROM loans l
JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
WHERE l.returned_on > l.due_on;

Rohan returned *The Alchemist* three days late.

8. Loans per genre

SELECT b.genre, COUNT(*) AS loans
FROM loans l
JOIN books b ON b.id = l.book_id
GROUP BY b.genre
ORDER BY loans DESC;

9. Authors whose books were never borrowed

SELECT a.name
FROM authors a
JOIN books b      ON b.author_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.book_id = b.id
GROUP BY a.id, a.name
HAVING COUNT(l.id) = 0;

Empty: every author has at least one borrowed book. (*The Guide* was never borrowed, but its author's other book was.) Change the query to list books never borrowed instead.

Step 5: Day-to-day operations

-- Kabir borrows The Guide today
INSERT INTO loans (book_id, member_id, loaned_on, due_on)
VALUES (2, 4, '2024-06-10', '2024-06-24');

-- Asha returns Murder on the Orient Express
UPDATE loans
SET returned_on = '2024-06-10'
WHERE id = 2;

-- The library buys another copy of And Then There Were None
UPDATE books SET copies = copies + 1 WHERE id = 4;

Each statement targets exact rows by id. Try breaking the rules too: a loan for book 99, or a due date before the loan date. The constraints refuse them.

Ideas to extend it

  • Add a fines table: ₹5 per day late, calculated from returned_on - due_on.
  • Support books with several authors using a book_authors junction table.
  • Add a reservations table for books with no copies available.
  • Connect it to a program: the Python course shows how to query SQLite from Python.

What you've learned

In 15 lessons you've learned to design tables, protect data with constraints, insert, update and delete safely, filter, sort, group and join, and make it all fast with indexes. That's the SQL most developers and analysts use every day.

Summary

  • Good design starts with entities (authors, books, members) and relationships (loans).
  • Constraints and indexes are part of the design, not an afterthought.
  • JOINs, LEFT JOINs, GROUP BY and CASE answer real business questions.
  • Keep "today" as a parameter in practice queries; use the database's date function in real apps.

Next, continue with the Python course, where you'll write programs that work with data like this.
item.excerpt:encoded: Design, build and query a complete library database with authors, books, members and loans, using tables, constraints, joins, grouping and indexes.

item.title: How to Become an AI Engineer: A Step-by-Step Roadmap
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: an AI engineer builds software products that use AI models: chatbots, document search, automation, recommendations. The path is: solid programming (Python) → data and databases → web APIs → working with AI models through APIs → retrieval, evaluation and deployment → portfolio projects. You don't need a PhD; you need strong software skills plus a practical understanding of how models behave.

This roadmap is ordered so each stage builds on the last. Times assume about 10 hours a week; go faster or slower as your life allows.

What does an AI engineer actually do?

The title means different things at different companies, but most AI engineering work looks like this:

  • Connecting applications to AI models (language, vision, speech) through APIs.
  • Building retrieval systems so models can answer from company documents.
  • Designing prompts, tools and agents for multi-step tasks.
  • Evaluating quality: measuring accuracy, catching hallucinations, testing changes.
  • Handling the engineering: APIs, databases, cost, speed, monitoring, security and privacy.

It's different from related roles:

The AI engineer path is the most accessible for developers and career switchers, and the most in demand as companies add AI features.

Stage 1: Programming foundations (2–4 months)

Learn Python properly. AI engineering is software engineering first.

  • Variables, types, strings, lists, dictionaries, loops, functions.
  • Files, JSON, error handling, classes, modules, virtual environments and pip.
  • Git and GitHub (see our Git and GitHub for Beginners guide).

Follow our Python course from start to finish, including the expense tracker project.

Milestone: you can write a 200-line program that reads data, processes it and saves results, without copying code you don't understand.

Stage 2: Data and databases (1–2 months)

AI runs on data. You need to fetch, clean and store it.

  • SQL: SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, indexes. Our SQL course covers what you need.
  • pandas for working with tables in Python: loading CSVs, filtering, grouping, cleaning missing values.
  • Basic statistics: mean, median, distributions, and why averages can mislead.

Milestone: you can answer business questions from a database with SQL and clean a messy CSV with pandas.

Stage 3: Web and APIs (1–2 months)

AI features live inside applications, usually behind an API.

  • HTTP basics: requests, responses, status codes, JSON (our Python JSON and APIs lesson).
  • Build an API with FastAPI or Flask: endpoints, input validation, error handling.
  • Enough front-end to demo your work: basic HTML, CSS and JavaScript, or a quick UI library for Python.
  • Environment variables and secrets management.

Milestone: you've built and deployed a small API that others can call.

Stage 4: Working with AI models (1–2 months)

Now add AI.

  • How language models work: tokens, context windows, temperature, hallucinations (our explainer).
  • Calling model APIs from Python: messages, system instructions, streaming responses, handling errors and rate limits.
  • Prompt design for reliable output, including structured output like JSON (our prompting guide).
  • Tool use / function calling: letting a model call your functions.
  • Cost and speed: counting tokens, caching, choosing smaller models when they're enough.

Milestone: a small app where a model calls at least one tool you wrote, with error handling and a cost estimate.

Stage 5: Retrieval, agents and evaluation (2–3 months)

This is where AI engineering becomes its own discipline.

  • Embeddings: turning text into vectors so you can search by meaning.
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): splitting documents into chunks, embedding them, storing them (a vector database or a vector extension for PostgreSQL), retrieving the best matches and passing them to the model with the question.
  • Agents: loops of think → act → observe with tools, limits and human approval (What Are AI Agents?).
  • Evaluation: build a test set of questions with expected answers, measure accuracy, and check every change against it. This is the skill that separates demos from products.
  • Safety: prompt injection, data privacy, access control, and refusing out-of-scope requests.

Milestone: a "chat with your documents" app that cites its sources, plus an evaluation script showing how accurate it is.

Stage 6: Shipping like a professional (ongoing)

  • Deployment: Docker basics, a cloud platform, environment configuration.
  • Monitoring: logging requests, errors, latency and costs; collecting user feedback.
  • Testing: unit tests for your code, evaluation sets for AI behaviour.
  • Optional depth: fine-tuning basics, open-source models running locally, and the machine learning fundamentals (training, overfitting, metrics) that help you reason about model behaviour.

Portfolio projects that impress

Pick two or three and do them well, with a clear README, a demo video or link, and honest notes on limitations:

  1. Document Q&A with citations: answers questions about a set of PDFs (course notes, a product manual) and shows which passage each answer came from. Include accuracy numbers from your evaluation set.
  2. Support ticket triage: classifies incoming messages by topic and urgency, drafts a reply, and routes uncertain cases to a person.
  3. Data analyst agent: answers questions about a SQLite database by writing and running SQL, then explains the result, with read-only access only.
  4. Personal learning assistant: quizzes you on your notes using spaced repetition.

What hiring managers look for: real problems, clean code, tests, evaluation, sensible handling of errors and costs, and a clear explanation of trade-offs. A small, well-engineered project beats a flashy demo that breaks.

Getting your first role

  • Apply to software roles with AI features, not only roles titled "AI engineer". Many teams need developers who can ship AI features.
  • Write about what you build. Short posts explaining a problem you solved show communication skills, which matter a lot.
  • Contribute to open source: documentation, examples or small fixes in AI-related libraries.
  • Prepare for normal developer interviews: data structures basics, SQL, API design and debugging still come up.
  • Show judgement: in interviews, discuss when not to use AI, how you measured quality, and how you handled failures.

Common mistakes

  • Skipping fundamentals to jump straight into AI frameworks. When things break (and they will), fundamentals are how you fix them.
  • Only following tutorials. Build your own projects with your own data.
  • No evaluation. "It looks good when I try it" isn't enough.
  • Chasing every new tool. Frameworks change quickly; the underlying ideas (APIs, retrieval, evaluation, tools) last.
  • Ignoring security and privacy.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a computer science degree?

No. Many AI engineers come from other backgrounds. A degree helps with some employers, but a strong portfolio and solid fundamentals matter most for this role.

How much maths do I need?

For AI engineering: comfortable with basic algebra, percentages and statistics. Linear algebra and calculus become important if you move toward training models or research.

How long will this take?

At about 10 hours a week, roughly 9–15 months from zero to a job-ready portfolio. Prior programming experience shortens it a lot.

Should I learn machine learning theory first?

Learn enough to understand what models do and why they fail, alongside building. Deep theory is optional for AI engineering, and essential for ML research.

Summary

  • AI engineers build products with AI models; it's software engineering plus model know-how.
  • Path: Python → SQL and data → APIs → model APIs and prompting → RAG, agents and evaluation → deployment.
  • Prove skills with 2–3 well-engineered projects that include evaluation and honest limits.
  • Fundamentals and judgement outlast any specific tool or framework.
item.excerpt:encoded: A realistic roadmap to becoming an AI engineer: what the role involves, the skills to learn in order, projects that prove them, and how to land your first role.

item.title: How to Build a Developer Portfolio That Gets You Hired
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: a strong developer portfolio has 2–4 real projects that solve actual problems, each with a clear README, a live demo or video, clean code and tests, presented on a simple personal site and a tidy GitHub profile. Quality and explanation beat quantity.

When you don't have work experience, your portfolio is your experience. This guide shows how to choose projects, present them, and talk about them in interviews.

What employers look for

When a recruiter or developer looks at your portfolio, usually for just a few minutes, they want quick evidence of:

  1. You can build complete things, not just follow tutorials.
  2. Your code is readable, organised and tested.
  3. You can explain decisions: why this approach, what you'd improve.
  4. You care about users: a project that works, looks reasonable and handles errors.

Everything below serves those four points.

Choosing projects

Avoid the tutorial clones

Ten to-do apps and weather apps copied from tutorials show you can follow instructions, not that you can solve problems. If you build a common project, add something of your own: a feature, a twist, real data.

Solve real problems

The best projects come from real needs:

  • A tool for your family business, college club or local shop.
  • An automation that saves you time each week.
  • A dashboard for data you care about: cricket stats, your expenses, air quality in your city.
  • Something for a community you belong to.

Real problems give you real constraints, real users and a story for interviews.

Show range, with depth

A good set of 3 projects for a web developer might be:

  1. A polished front-end project: responsive, accessible, fast (e.g. a portfolio site or a product landing page).
  2. A full-stack app: front end + API + database + authentication (e.g. a habit tracker with accounts).
  3. A project in your target area: data, AI, mobile, or whatever role you want.

For AI-focused roles, see the project ideas in our AI Engineer Roadmap.

Finish them

A finished, small project beats an ambitious unfinished one. Define a small first version, ship it, then improve.

Making each project shine

The README is your project's front page

Most people will only read the README. Include:

# Project name
One sentence: what it does and who it's for.

Live demo: https://…   |   Video: https://…

## Screenshot
[image]

## Features
- …

## Tech stack
Python, FastAPI, SQLite, HTML/CSS/JS

## How to run it locally
1. git clone …
2. python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
3. pip install -r requirements.txt
4. python app.py

## What I learned / challenges
- How I handled …
- Why I chose … over …

## What I'd improve next
- …

The "challenges" and "what I'd improve" sections show maturity and give interviewers easy questions to ask.

A live demo or video

Deploy it if you can (static sites for free on GitHub Pages, Netlify or similar; small back-ends on free or cheap platforms). If deployment isn't practical, record a 1–2 minute video walkthrough. Nobody will install your project just to see it.

Clean code

  • Consistent formatting (use a formatter like Prettier or Black).
  • Meaningful names; no leftover debug prints or commented-out blocks.
  • A sensible folder structure.
  • A .gitignore, and no secrets in the repository.
  • Some tests, even a few, for the important logic.

Honest commit history

Small, clearly described commits ("Add password reset email", "Fix date sorting bug") show how you work. One giant "final version" commit hides it.

Use of AI

Using AI tools is normal. Be ready to explain every part of your code, and mention in the README if AI helped and how you reviewed its output. Being unable to explain your own project in an interview is a red flag.

Your portfolio website

Keep it simple and fast:

  • Home: your name, what you do in one line ("Front-end developer who builds accessible websites for small businesses"), and links to your best projects.
  • Projects: a card per project with an image, one-line description, tech stack, and links to demo and code.
  • About: a short, genuine story: how you got into coding, what you enjoy building, what you're looking for.
  • Contact: email and LinkedIn/GitHub links.

Building the site yourself is itself a project. Our HTML and CSS projects walk you through a personal profile page you can extend into a portfolio.

Make sure it works on phones, loads quickly, and has no broken links. A slow or broken portfolio site hurts more than not having one.

Your GitHub profile

  • Pin your best 4–6 repositories.
  • Add a short profile README: who you are, what you're learning, how to contact you.
  • Archive or make private old experiments you don't want judged.
  • Regular activity is nice, but quality projects matter far more than a green contribution graph.

Talking about your projects

In interviews, you'll often be asked "tell me about a project". Prepare a 2-minute story for each one:

  1. Problem: what it solves and for whom.
  2. Your solution: the main features and tech choices.
  3. A challenge: something hard and how you solved it.
  4. The result: users, time saved, what it taught you.
  5. Next steps: what you'd improve with more time.

Be ready for follow-ups: "Why did you choose SQLite?", "How would this handle 10,000 users?", "How did you test it?". Honest answers like "I'd add caching and move to PostgreSQL, because…" are far better than pretending it's perfect.

Common mistakes

  • Too many unfinished or tutorial projects.
  • No README, or a default one.
  • Broken demo links.
  • API keys or passwords committed to GitHub. Remove them and rotate the keys immediately if this happens.
  • A portfolio site that doesn't work on mobile.
  • Listing every technology you've touched instead of what you can actually use.

A 6-week plan

Then keep improving one project at a time while applying for roles.

Frequently asked questions

How many projects do I need?

Two to four strong ones. More isn't better if they're shallow.

Do I need a custom domain?

It's a nice touch and cheap, but not required. A working site on a free subdomain is fine.

Should I include group or college projects?

Yes, if you describe your part clearly. Team experience is valuable.

What if my projects aren't impressive?

Make them better rather than more numerous: add tests, handle errors, improve the design, deploy them, write a great README. Polish is impressive.

Summary

  • 2–4 finished projects that solve real problems beat many tutorial clones.
  • Every project needs a strong README, a demo or video, clean code and no secrets.
  • Keep your portfolio site and GitHub simple, fast and focused on your best work.
  • Prepare a short story for each project: problem, solution, challenge, result, next steps.
item.excerpt:encoded: Build a portfolio that proves your skills: which projects to choose, how to write READMEs, what to put on your portfolio site and GitHub, and how to present your work in interviews.

item.title: Skills Every Developer Needs in the Age of AI
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: as AI makes writing code faster, the valuable skills shift toward everything around writing code: understanding the problem, reading and judging code, debugging, testing, designing systems, security, communication and knowledge of the business. Fundamentals become more important, not less, because they're how you judge AI output.

Here are the skills worth investing in, why they matter now, and how to build each one.

1. Strong fundamentals

AI can produce a sorting function in seconds. Knowing whether it's correct, efficient and appropriate requires understanding the basics:

  • Data types, control flow, functions and scope.
  • Data structures: lists/arrays, dictionaries/maps, sets, and when each is the right tool.
  • How the web works: HTTP, requests and responses, HTML/CSS/JavaScript in the browser.
  • Databases and SQL.
  • Basic performance ideas: why a loop inside a loop over large data is slow.

How to build it: finish a structured course in one language (our JavaScript or Python course), doing the exercises yourself before using AI.

2. Framing problems clearly

The quality of AI output depends on the quality of the request. Developers who can turn a vague idea into a precise specification (inputs, outputs, edge cases, constraints) get far better results from AI tools and from teammates.

How to build it: before coding anything, write three things: what it should do, an example input and output, and two edge cases. Practise writing precise prompts (our prompting guide).

3. Reading and reviewing code

As more code is generated, developers spend more time reading than writing. Reviewing well means spotting:

  • Logic errors and unhandled edge cases.
  • Security problems: unvalidated input, injection, exposed secrets.
  • Code that works but is hard to maintain.
  • "Hallucinated" functions or outdated APIs.

How to build it: read open-source code in projects you use. Review AI-generated code line by line and list everything you'd change. Ask to review classmates' or colleagues' pull requests.

4. Debugging

Every program breaks. Debugging is systematic thinking: reproduce the problem, form a hypothesis, test it, narrow it down. AI can suggest causes, but you need to verify them and understand the system well enough to know where to look.

How to build it: when you hit a bug, write down your hypothesis before changing anything. Learn your debugger (breakpoints, stepping, watching variables) and read error messages fully, starting from the last line.

5. Testing

Tests are how you know code works, especially code you didn't write yourself. They also make AI agents much more useful, because "make the tests pass" is a clear, checkable goal.

  • Unit tests for functions, with normal, edge and invalid inputs.
  • Integration tests for parts working together.
  • For AI features: evaluation sets that measure answer quality.

How to build it: add tests to every project from now on. When AI generates code, write (or at least review) the tests yourself.

6. System design

Choosing how pieces fit together (what goes in the database, which service calls which, how to handle failures, what happens with ten times more users) is judgement that AI can't fully provide, because it depends on your context, team and constraints.

How to build it: for each project, draw a simple diagram of the parts and data flow. Read about common designs: caching, queues, background jobs, authentication. Ask "what if this fails?" for every component.

7. Security and privacy awareness

AI-generated code repeats insecure patterns it learned from the internet, and AI features bring new risks like prompt injection and data leakage. Developers who think about security by default are increasingly valuable.

  • Validate input; use parameterised SQL queries.
  • Keep secrets out of code and repositories.
  • Apply least privilege, especially to AI agents with tools.
  • Know what data may and may not be sent to external services.

How to build it: read the OWASP Top 10 (a list of common web security risks) and check your own projects against it.

8. Working effectively with AI tools

Using AI well is itself a skill: giving context, asking for small pieces, iterating, verifying, and knowing when not to use it. See How to Use AI Coding Assistants Without Losing Your Skills.

How to build it: use an assistant on real projects with a strict rule: never commit code you can't explain.

9. Communication

Explaining trade-offs to a manager, writing clear documentation, describing a bug precisely, discussing requirements with non-technical people: these skills matter more as routine coding gets automated. Clear writing also directly improves your AI prompts.

How to build it: write a README for every project, and short posts about problems you solved. Explain a technical topic to a non-technical friend.

10. Domain knowledge

A developer who understands healthcare, finance, logistics or education, and can code, is far more valuable than one who only codes. Domain knowledge tells you which problems matter, what "correct" means and which edge cases are dangerous.

How to build it: pick an industry you find interesting (or already work in) and build projects for its real problems.

11. Learning how to learn

Tools and frameworks change every year. The lasting skill is learning new ones quickly: reading documentation, building a small test project, and connecting new ideas to what you already know.

How to build it: each month, learn one new tool by building something tiny with it from the official docs. Use AI as a tutor, not a replacement (our guide).

What matters less than before

  • Memorising syntax and library function names: tools help with recall.
  • Writing large amounts of boilerplate by hand.
  • Knowing one framework deeply but nothing else.

They still help, but they're no longer what sets a developer apart.

A simple self-check

Rate yourself from 1 to 5 on each skill:

Pick your two lowest scores and focus on them for the next month.

Frequently asked questions

Is it still worth learning to code?

Yes. Code is how ideas become working software, and understanding it is what lets you direct and check AI tools. The job is changing, not disappearing.

Should I specialise or be a generalist?

Build broad fundamentals first, then go deep in one area (front-end, back-end, data, AI engineering) while staying curious about the others. "T-shaped" developers are in demand.

What's one habit that improves most of these skills?

Building real projects end to end: planning, coding, testing, deploying and writing about them. Each project exercises almost every skill on this list.

Summary

  • AI speeds up writing code; the value shifts to judging, designing, testing and communicating.
  • Fundamentals matter more, because they're how you evaluate AI output.
  • Invest in problem framing, code review, debugging, testing, system design and security.
  • Communication, domain knowledge and learning how to learn keep you valuable as tools change.
item.excerpt:encoded: Which developer skills matter more now that AI writes code: fundamentals, problem framing, reading code, debugging, testing, system design, security, communication and domain knowledge.

item.title: How to Use AI Coding Assistants Without Losing Your Skills
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: use an AI coding assistant as a fast, knowledgeable pair programmer: let it draft, explain and test, but you stay responsible for understanding, reviewing and running every line. Used that way, it speeds you up and teaches you. Used as a copy-paste machine, it slows your learning and ships bugs.

AI coding assistants come in a few forms: chat assistants in the browser, autocomplete inside your editor, and agents that can edit files and run commands in your project. This guide applies to all of them.

What AI assistants are genuinely good at

  • Boilerplate: HTML skeletons, config files, repetitive CRUD code, test scaffolding.
  • Explaining: "What does this regex do?", "Explain this error", "Walk me through this function line by line."
  • Translating: a loop into a list comprehension, JavaScript into Python, SQL into plain English.
  • Generating tests and edge cases you hadn't thought of.
  • Reviewing: spotting likely bugs, missing error handling and security issues.
  • Getting unstuck: suggesting three approaches when you don't know where to start.
  • Documentation: docstrings, README sections, comments for tricky code.

Where they go wrong

  • Plausible but wrong code: it runs, but handles an edge case incorrectly.
  • Invented APIs: functions, options or packages that don't exist, or existed in an older version.
  • Outdated patterns: code that was common years ago, like insecure practices or deprecated functions.
  • Security mistakes: SQL built with string concatenation, missing input validation, secrets in code.
  • Missing context: it doesn't know your whole codebase, your conventions or your business rules unless you show them.
  • Overconfidence: it rarely says "I'm not sure".

None of this makes the tools useless. It means review is part of the job.

A safe workflow

1. Think first

Before asking, spend two minutes deciding what you want: inputs, outputs, edge cases. Write it down. This makes your prompt better and keeps you in charge of the design. (See How to Write Better AI Prompts.)

2. Give context

Paste the relevant code, the exact error, the language and version, and the constraints: "Python 3.12, standard library only, keep the function signature".

3. Ask for small pieces

One function, one component, one bug at a time. Large generated chunks are hard to review and hide mistakes.

4. Read every line

If you don't understand a line, ask: "Explain line 7." Never commit code you couldn't explain to a teammate.

5. Run it and test it

Run the code. Try normal input, empty input, wrong input, huge input. Ask the assistant for test cases, then check that those tests are actually meaningful.

6. Check against official docs

For library functions and options, confirm in the official documentation (MDN for web, docs.python.org, the library's own docs). This catches invented or outdated APIs.

7. Review for security

Ask yourself (or the assistant): where does input come from? Is it validated? Are queries parameterised? Are secrets out of the code? Are errors handled?

A worked example

You ask: *"Write a Python function that reads a CSV of products and returns the total stock value."*

The assistant returns:

def total_value(path):
    total = 0
    for line in open(path):
        name, price, stock = line.split(",")
        total += float(price) * int(stock)
    return total

It looks fine and may work on a simple file. A careful review finds four problems:

  1. The header row would crash float("price").
  2. Splitting on commas breaks for names like "Backpack, large".
  3. The file is never closed (no with).
  4. Bad rows crash the whole function.

A better version, after follow-up prompts and your review:

import csv

def total_value(path):
    """Return the total of price * stock for every valid row in a products CSV."""
    total = 0.0
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            try:
                total += float(row["price"]) * int(row["stock"])
            except (KeyError, ValueError):
                continue  # skip malformed rows
    return total

The assistant helped, but the quality came from your questions. Knowing about CSV quoting, with and exceptions (all covered in our Python Files lesson) is what let you spot the problems.

Habits that keep you learning

AI can make you faster today and weaker tomorrow if you're not careful. These habits keep your skills growing:

  • Try first, then ask. Spend 15–20 minutes on a problem before asking. Struggle is how learning sticks.
  • Ask for hints, not answers. "Give me a hint about why this loop never ends" teaches more than a fixed loop.
  • Ask "why". After getting a solution, ask why it works and what alternatives exist.
  • Retype instead of pasting when learning something new.
  • Explain it back. Write a comment in your own words explaining the code. If you can't, you don't understand it yet.
  • Do some practice without AI. Exercises at the end of each lesson on VitalStack are best done on your own first.

Using assistants in a team

  • Follow your team's rules on which tools are allowed and what code or data can be shared.
  • Never paste secrets, credentials or customer data.
  • Mention AI-generated code in reviews if your team expects it.
  • Code review standards don't change: AI-written code gets the same scrutiny as human-written code.

Prompts worth saving

Explain this code line by line for someone who knows basic [language]: [code]

What are the edge cases this function doesn't handle? Don't fix them yet,
just list them: [code]

Write unit tests for this function covering normal input, empty input
and invalid input: [code]

Review this for security issues (injection, validation, secrets, error
handling). List issues by severity: [code]

I want to solve [problem] myself. Give me a hint, not the solution.

Frequently asked questions

Is it cheating to use AI while learning?

Not if you use it to understand rather than to avoid thinking. Asking for explanations, hints and reviews is like having a tutor. Copying answers you don't understand is what hurts you, in interviews and on the job.

Will AI assistants replace junior developers?

They change what junior developers do. Routine code is faster, so the value moves to understanding problems, reviewing, testing, debugging and communicating. Juniors who build strong fundamentals and use AI well can contribute faster than ever.

Which assistant is best?

They improve constantly, so any specific ranking ages quickly. Choose one that integrates with your editor, supports your languages and is allowed by your school or employer. The workflow in this guide matters more than the brand.

Should I trust the code if the tests pass?

Only if the tests are good. Generated tests sometimes test the wrong thing or mirror the bug. Read the tests too, and add cases for edge conditions yourself.

Summary

  • AI assistants are excellent for drafting, explaining, translating, testing and reviewing code.
  • They can produce plausible but wrong, outdated or insecure code.
  • Work in small pieces, read every line, run and test it, and check official docs.
  • Keep learning: try first, ask for hints, ask why, and practise without AI regularly.
item.excerpt:encoded: Get real value from AI coding assistants: what they're good and bad at, a safe workflow for generating and reviewing code, and habits that keep you learning.

item.title: How to Write Better AI Prompts: A Practical Guide
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: a good prompt gives the AI what a smart new colleague would need: the goal, the context, the constraints, the format you want, and ideally an example. Vague prompts get generic answers; specific prompts get useful ones.

AI assistants are only as helpful as the instructions they receive. This guide gives you a simple framework and real before-and-after examples you can adapt today.

Why prompts matter

A language model predicts a likely response to your text (see How Large Language Models Work). If your prompt could mean ten different things, you'll get an average of all ten. If it's precise, the most likely response is the one you actually want.

Compare:

Weak:   Write about Python.

Strong: Write a 150-word introduction to Python for a complete beginner
        who wants to analyse sales data in Excel. Mention one thing Python
        does better than Excel, avoid jargon, and end with a suggested first step.

The second prompt answers every question the AI would otherwise guess: who it's for, how long, what to include, what tone, how to end.

The framework: G-C-C-F-E

Goal: what do you want?

Start with the task in one clear sentence. Use action verbs: *explain, write, fix, compare, summarise, list, rewrite, review*.

Context: what does it need to know?

Who's the audience? What have you already tried? What's the situation? The AI knows nothing about your project, your level or your constraints unless you say so.

Constraints: what are the rules?

Length, tone, language, things to avoid, tools or versions to use: "Use only the standard library", "no more than 5 bullet points", "keep my original meaning".

Format: how should the answer look?

Bullet list, table, numbered steps, code only, JSON with specific keys, an email ready to send. If you'll paste the answer somewhere, say how it needs to look.

Example: show what good looks like

One short example often beats a paragraph of description. Show the style, structure or output you want.

You don't need all five every time. For quick questions, goal plus context is often enough. For anything you'll reuse or publish, use all five.

Before and after: coding

Weak:
My code doesn't work, fix it.
[code]

Strong:
This Python function should return the average of a list of numbers,
but it crashes with "ZeroDivisionError" when the list is empty.

[code]

1. Explain in one sentence why it crashes.
2. Fix it so an empty list returns 0.
3. Keep the function name and signature the same.
4. Add two quick test cases using assert.

What changed: the expected behaviour, the exact error, the constraint (same signature) and the output format (explanation, fix, tests).

Tip: always paste the exact error message and say what you expected to happen. "It doesn't work" forces the AI to guess.

Before and after: learning a concept

Weak:
Explain recursion.

Strong:
I'm learning JavaScript and understand loops and functions, but recursion
confuses me. Explain recursion using a real-life analogy first, then a
simple JavaScript example that counts down from 5, then show me the same
thing as a loop so I can compare. Finish with one practice exercise
(without the answer).

Asking for an analogy, a comparison with something you already know, and an exercise turns the AI into a tutor instead of an encyclopaedia.

Before and after: writing

Weak:
Write an email to my manager about leave.

Strong:
Write a short, polite email to my manager, Priya, asking for leave on
the 14th and 15th for a family wedding. I've already finished the report
due that week and Rohan has agreed to cover urgent messages. Tone: friendly
but professional. Under 120 words. Include a subject line.

The details make the email ready to send, instead of a template full of [brackets].

Before and after: data tasks

Weak:
Analyse this data.

Strong:
Below is CSV data of monthly sales (columns: month, region, revenue).
1. Which region grew the most from the first to the last month, in %?
2. Are there any months that look like errors or outliers?
3. Give the answer as a short table, then 2–3 sentences of insight.
If something can't be determined from the data, say so instead of guessing.

[data]

The last line is important: give the AI permission to say "I don't know". It reduces made-up answers.

Techniques that work

Assign a role (lightly)

"Act as a senior Python reviewer" or "You're a patient tutor for beginners" sets the tone and depth. It helps, but specifics about the task matter more than the role.

Ask for steps before the answer

For reasoning problems, "work through this step by step, then give the final answer" often improves accuracy, and lets you see where it went wrong.

Break big tasks into smaller prompts

Instead of "build me a complete website", go step by step: plan the pages → write the HTML for the home page → add the CSS → add the contact form. You stay in control and can correct course early.

Iterate: the first answer is a draft

Reply with what to change: "Shorter", "more examples", "use a table", "the second point is wrong because…". Conversation is part of prompting.

Ask it to ask you questions

"Before you answer, ask me up to 3 questions about anything that's unclear." Great for plans, designs and anything personal.

Use delimiters for pasted content

Separate instructions from material with clear markers:

Summarise the article between the triple quotes in 5 bullet points
for a busy executive.

"""
[article text]
"""

This helps the model tell your instructions apart from the content.

Prompts to save and reuse

Code review:
Review this [language] code for bugs, security issues and readability.
List problems in order of importance, with a fix for each. Don't rewrite
the whole file. [code]

Explain an error:
I got this error: [error]. Here's the code: [code]. Explain what it means
in plain English, the most likely cause, and how to fix it.

Study plan:
Create a [n]-week plan to learn [topic] for someone who knows [current
skills] and has [hours] hours a week. Include weekly goals and one small
project per week.

Summarise:
Summarise the text below in [n] bullet points for [audience]. Keep numbers
and names exact. [text]

Limits to remember

  • Check facts and code. A great prompt reduces errors but doesn't remove them. Run the code; verify claims that matter.
  • Don't paste secrets (passwords, API keys, private customer data) into AI tools unless your organisation allows it.
  • Your judgement is the final step, especially for anything published, legal, medical or financial.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need special "magic words"?

No. Clear, specific, complete instructions beat tricks. Write as you would to a capable colleague who knows nothing about your situation.

Should prompts be long?

As long as needed, no longer. Add details that change the answer; skip filler like "please kindly".

Why do I get different answers to the same prompt?

Models use some randomness when generating text. If you need consistency, be more specific, give an example of the exact format, or ask for a fixed structure.

Is prompt engineering a real job skill?

Yes, as part of other jobs. Developers building AI features, writers, analysts and support teams all benefit from writing clear prompts. It's really the skill of clear communication.

Summary

  • Good prompts include Goal, Context, Constraints, Format and an Example.
  • Paste exact errors, define the audience, and specify the output format.
  • Break big tasks into steps, iterate on drafts, and let the AI ask clarifying questions.
  • Give permission to say "I don't know", and always verify important output.
item.excerpt:encoded: A practical framework for writing prompts that get useful answers from AI assistants, with before-and-after examples for coding, writing, learning and data tasks.

item.title: How to Use AI to Learn Programming Faster
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: treat AI as a patient personal tutor, not an answer machine. Use it to explain concepts at your level, quiz you, give hints when you're stuck, and review your code, while you still write the code yourself.

Learning to code used to mean getting stuck alone for hours. Now you can get an explanation, a hint or a review in seconds. That's a huge advantage, if you use it in a way that builds skills instead of replacing them. Here's a study system that works.

The core rule: you write the code

Research on learning consistently shows that we remember what we actively produce, not what we passively read. An AI that writes all your code feels productive, but your brain does none of the work. So:

  • AI explains, quizzes, hints and reviews.
  • You design, type, run, debug and fix.

Keep that split and AI will roughly double your learning speed.

Step 1: Follow a structured course

AI is great at answering questions, but bad at deciding what you should learn next. Follow a course with a clear order, such as the VitalStack paths: HTML → CSS → JavaScript, or straight to Python for data and AI. Use the AI alongside each lesson, not instead of it.

Step 2: Get explanations at your level

When a lesson doesn't click, ask for a different explanation. Tell the AI what you already know:

I'm on lesson 13 of a JavaScript course. I understand arrays and loops
but not array methods like map and filter. Explain map using a real-life
analogy, then one tiny example, then compare it to the for loop I'd
normally write.

Useful variations:

  • "Explain it like I'm 12."
  • "Explain it with a cooking analogy."
  • "Show me the most common mistake beginners make with this."
  • "What's the difference between X and Y, in a table?"

Step 3: Practise with generated exercises

Courses have a limited number of exercises. AI can make unlimited ones, matched to your level:

Give me 5 practice exercises on Python dictionaries, from easy to
medium. Don't include the answers. After I send my solutions, review
them one by one.

Do them in your own editor, run them, then paste your solutions for feedback. This "practise → feedback" loop is the fastest way to improve.

Step 4: Debug with hints, not fixes

When your code breaks, resist asking for the fix. Ask for a hint:

My code should print the even numbers from a list but prints nothing.
Don't give me the corrected code. Give me one hint about where to look.

[your code]
[what you expected vs what happened]

If one hint isn't enough, ask for a second, more specific hint. Finding the bug yourself, even with help, teaches you the debugging skill you'll use for the rest of your career.

Also learn to read errors yourself first: copy the last line of the error, try to understand it, and only then ask: "I think this error means X. Am I right?"

Step 5: Get code reviews

Once your code works, ask how to make it better:

Here's my solution to an exercise. It works. Review it like a friendly
senior developer: is anything wrong, unclear or non-idiomatic? Suggest
improvements but explain why, and keep my overall approach.

You'll learn idioms (the "natural" way to write things in a language) much faster than from reading alone.

Step 6: Build small projects with AI as a mentor

Projects are where knowledge becomes skill. Use AI to plan, not to build:

I've finished HTML and CSS and 10 JavaScript lessons. Suggest 3 small
project ideas I could finish in a weekend. For the one I choose, break
it into 5 milestones, but don't write the code.

Then build milestone by milestone, asking for hints and reviews along the way. Good beginner projects: a tip calculator, a quiz, a to-do list (like our JavaScript project), a personal portfolio, an expense tracker (like our Python project).

Step 7: Review with spaced repetition

You forget quickly unless you review. Once a week:

Quiz me with 10 short questions on what I've learned this week: Python
lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries. Ask one question at a time and
wait for my answer before giving feedback.

Questions you get wrong tell you exactly what to revise.

A weekly routine that works

Consistency matters far more than long sessions. One focused hour a day beats a seven-hour weekend binge.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Copy-pasting solutions you don't understand.
  • Asking before trying. Give yourself 15–20 minutes of honest effort first.
  • Endless tutorial mode. Reading and asking without building projects.
  • Trusting everything. AI can be wrong; run the code and check official docs when something seems off.
  • Skipping fundamentals because "AI can write it". You need fundamentals to judge what AI writes.

Frequently asked questions

Can I learn programming only with AI?

You can, but a structured course plus AI is faster and leaves fewer gaps. The course gives the path; the AI gives personal help along it.

How long does it take to learn to code with AI help?

For the basics of one language (variables to functions and small projects), about 2–3 months at an hour a day is realistic. Becoming job-ready usually takes 6–12 months of steady practice and projects.

Which language should I start with?

For websites, start with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. For data, automation and AI, start with Python. Both are excellent first languages.

Is it okay to use AI in exercises?

Try every exercise yourself first. Then use AI to check, explain mistakes and suggest improvements.

Summary

  • Use AI as a tutor: explanations, exercises, hints, reviews and quizzes.
  • Keep the core rule: you write and debug the code.
  • Follow a structured course and build small projects from early on.
  • Review weekly with AI quizzes, and stay consistent with daily practice.
item.excerpt:encoded: A step-by-step study system for learning to code with an AI tutor: explanations at your level, practice questions, debugging help, project feedback and spaced review.

item.title: How Large Language Models Work (Without the Maths)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: a large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on enormous amounts of text to do one thing: predict the next piece of text. Repeating that prediction, piece by piece, lets it write answers, code, summaries and conversations.

That sounds too simple to explain what chat assistants can do. This guide shows how such a simple goal leads to such capable behaviour, and why the same mechanism explains their mistakes.

Step 1: Text becomes tokens

Models don't read letters or whole words. Text is split into tokens: common words, parts of words, punctuation and spaces.

"Learning Python is fun!"  →  ["Learning", " Python", " is", " fun", "!"]
"unbelievably"             →  ["un", "believ", "ably"]

Each token is mapped to a number, and each number to a list of values (a vector) that captures something about its meaning. Words used in similar ways end up with similar vectors: "cat" is closer to "dog" than to "carburettor".

Why it matters to you: usage limits, prices and the model's memory are all measured in tokens. In English, a token averages roughly three-quarters of a word; other languages and code often use more tokens for the same content.

Step 2: Predict the next token

Given some text, the model calculates a probability for every possible next token:

Input:  "The capital of France is"
Output: " Paris" 92%   " a" 3%   " located" 2%   ...

It picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats:

"The capital of France is" → " Paris" → "." → " It" → " is" → " known" → ...

That's the whole generation process: one token at a time, each chosen based on everything before it. A long answer is thousands of these predictions in a row.

Step 3: How it learned to predict so well

Pre-training

The model starts with random parameters (billions of adjustable numbers) and reads a huge collection of text: books, websites, code, articles. For each position, it guesses the next token, checks the real one, and adjusts its parameters slightly to make the right answer more likely. Repeated trillions of times, this forces the model to absorb grammar, facts, writing styles, programming patterns and a great deal of reasoning-like structure, because all of those help predict text.

To predict the next line of a Python function, it helps to "know" Python. To predict the end of a maths explanation, it helps to follow the steps. Capability emerges from prediction.

The transformer and attention

Most LLMs use an architecture called the transformer. Its key idea is attention: when processing each token, the model looks at all the other tokens in the text and decides which ones matter most. In "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big", attention helps link "it" to "trophy". Stacking many layers of attention lets the model connect ideas across long passages.

Fine-tuning and feedback

A pre-trained model is a powerful text predictor but not a helpful assistant: ask it a question and it might continue with more questions. So it's further trained on examples of good conversations, and refined with feedback from people (and other techniques) that reward helpful, accurate and safe answers. This step turns a predictor into an assistant.

The context window: the model's working memory

The model only "sees" the text currently in its context window: your messages, its replies, any documents you pasted, and instructions from the app. That's measured in tokens and is limited, though modern windows are large.

Practical consequences:

  • In a very long conversation, early details may fall out of the window or get less attention.
  • The model doesn't remember previous conversations unless the app stores and re-inserts them.
  • Giving the relevant information in the prompt is the most reliable way to get accurate answers about your specific situation.

Temperature: why answers vary

When choosing the next token, the model doesn't always pick the most likely one. A setting often called temperature controls randomness:

  • Low temperature: picks likely tokens; more predictable and focused. Good for code and facts.
  • High temperature: more varied choices; more creative, but more likely to go off track.

That's why asking the same question twice can give different answers.

Why LLMs "hallucinate"

An LLM generates plausible text. Usually plausible and true overlap, because it learned from lots of accurate writing. But when it lacks the information, it doesn't stop; it produces text that sounds right: a confident fake citation, an API function that doesn't exist, a wrong date.

Ways to reduce this:

  • Give it the source material and ask it to answer only from that.
  • Ask for sources or reasoning you can check.
  • Use tools: many assistants can search the web, run code or query databases, grounding answers in real data.
  • Verify anything important: run the code, check the docs, confirm the facts.

What LLMs are great at

  • Drafting, rewriting and summarising text.
  • Explaining concepts at different levels ("explain recursion to a 12-year-old").
  • Writing and explaining code, generating tests, finding likely bugs.
  • Transforming formats: notes to email, JSON to a table, English to Hindi.
  • Brainstorming options and asking you good questions.

Where to be careful

  • Exact facts, numbers, legal or medical advice: check them.
  • Maths and long precise procedures: ask it to use a code or calculation tool, or check the result.
  • Recent events: the model's knowledge stops at its training date unless connected to live sources.
  • Private data: follow your organisation's rules about what you paste into AI tools.

How developers use LLMs in apps

Applications call LLMs through an API: send a prompt (and settings), get text back. Common patterns:

  • Prompting with instructions: a "system" message that defines the assistant's role and rules.
  • Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): search your own documents for relevant passages, put them in the prompt, and ask the model to answer from them. This is how "chat with your docs" tools work.
  • Tool use / function calling: the model decides to call functions you provide (search, calculator, database), and you return the results to it.
  • Agents: a model that plans and takes several steps with tools to complete a task. See What Are AI Agents?.

If you know Python, calling an LLM API is a few lines of code, which makes the Python course a great starting point.

Frequently asked questions

Does the model search the internet for every answer?

Not by itself. The base model answers from patterns learned in training. Some apps add a search tool and pass the results to the model.

Does an LLM understand what it says?

It builds rich internal representations of language and concepts, which is why it can be so useful, but it doesn't have beliefs or experiences like a person. Treat it as a very capable pattern-based tool, not an authority.

Why does it sometimes get simple things wrong, like counting letters?

Tokens: the model sees "strawberry" as a few chunks, not individual letters, so letter-level tasks are surprisingly hard for it. Asking it to write and run code for such tasks works far better.

Is bigger always better?

Larger models are generally more capable, but smaller ones are faster and cheaper, and are often good enough for focused tasks. Many products use a mix.

Summary

  • LLMs split text into tokens and predict the next token, one at a time.
  • They learn by predicting text across enormous datasets, then are fine-tuned to be helpful.
  • The context window is their working memory; temperature controls randomness.
  • They can hallucinate because they generate plausible text; give them sources and verify important output.
  • Developers use them through APIs with patterns like RAG, tool use and agents.
item.excerpt:encoded: A clear explanation of large language models: tokens, next-word prediction, training, context windows, temperature, why they hallucinate, and how to use them well.

item.title: What Are AI Agents? How They Work and When to Use Them
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Short answer: an AI agent is a system where a language model doesn't just answer once, but works in a loop: it decides what to do next, uses tools (search, code, files, APIs) to do it, looks at the result, and repeats until the task is complete.

A chatbot answers questions. An agent gets things done: "find the three cheapest flights and put them in a spreadsheet", "fix the failing test in this project", "research these five companies and summarise them". This guide explains how agents work, where they're useful, and where they go wrong.

From chatbot to agent

The three ingredients

1. A model that can reason about steps

A large language model (see How Large Language Models Work) reads the goal, the conversation so far and the tool results, and decides the next action.

2. Tools

Tools are functions the agent can call. The developer describes each tool (its name, what it does, its inputs), and the model can ask to use it:

Tool: search_web(query)        → returns search results
Tool: read_file(path)          → returns file contents
Tool: run_python(code)         → returns the output
Tool: send_email(to, subject, body)

The model doesn't run the tool itself. It outputs a structured request like search_web("best laptops under 60000 rupees"); the application runs it and passes the result back. This is often called tool use or function calling.

3. The loop

1. Read the goal and everything so far
2. Decide: answer now, or call a tool?
3. If a tool: run it, add the result to the context
4. Go back to 1
